title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
summary: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous-submission-20.github.io/T-WLA.github.io/.

Keywords: Robot foundation models; Vision–language–action models (VLA); World-action models (WAM); Visuotactile Manipulation; Residual Action Correction. Introduction sec:introduction Contact-rich manipulation refers to tasks whose success depends on precisely managing physical contact with objects or the surrounding environment~ hogan2022contact,lee2019making . Tactile feedback complements vision by revealing local contact conditions that are difficult to infer from images alone niu2026t,song2025opentouch,xue2025reactive,zhou2026touchworld . For example, when inserting a plug into a socket, vision guides alignment and approach, while touch provides feedback on contact and insertion resistance. Because these conditions can change between visual updates, tactile feedback supports rapid corrections to the ongoing motion. Despite the importance of tactile feedback in contact-rich manipulation, many general-purpose robot policies rely primarily on vision. Vision--language--action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision--language backbones to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions kim2024openvla,intelligence2025pi_ . World--action models further integrate future-state prediction with action generation, linking control decisions to the anticipated evolution of the environment rift2026wam,yuan2026fastwam . Without tactile feedback, these models must infer local contact conditions from visual cues, which may limit their response to visually subtle contact changes during precise manipulation. Recent work incorporates tactile feedback into robot control through variable-rate expert architectures niu2026t , residual adaptation wang2026vitar , and inference-time policy steering wu2026inference . We investigate a complementary question: how can fast tactile feedback correct a slow visual policy between visual updates? Our central idea is to generate asynchronous tactile corrections conditioned on persistent visual memory. The visual branch processes RGB observations at 39.7~Hz, producing a base action chunk and a history-aware visual memory at each update. The tactile branch processes touch at 119.1~Hz, combining recent tactile context with the cached visual memory and the active action chunk to predict residual corrections to its remaining, unexecuted actions. This allows contact feedback to refine ongoing motion without waiting for the next visual update or rerunning the visual branch. We instantiate this idea in , a multi-rate architecture for asynchronous visual--tactile control (Fig.~ fig:overview ). The visual branch generates an action chunk and a history-aware visual representation, which is cached until the next visual update. Between these updates, a lightweight tactile editor combines the cached representation with recent tactile observations to produce high-frequency residual corrections to the ongoing action chunk. This separation allows the controller to respond to changing contact conditions without repeatedly running the visual branch. During training, future-image and future-pressure prediction regularize the control representations, encouraging them to capture information relevant to subsequent interactions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Memory-guided asynchronous control. We propose , which uses the same history-aware visual memory to guide base-action generation and tactile correction. A lightweight tactile editor uses this memory and the active action chunk to correct unexecuted actions between visual updates, without rerunning the visual branch. Predictive supervision for control. We regularize the visual memory through future-image prediction and the tactile features through both future-image and future-pressure prediction. These auxiliary objectives complement action supervision, and their prediction heads are removed at inference. Evaluation across hand-motion prediction and robot manipulation. Experiments on EgoTouch and Tachin show improved finger-joint prediction accuracy, while real-robot tests show that increases mean task success from 17.0 to 50.0 . Ablations examine the contributions of tactile input, visual history, and predictive supervision. Related work sec:related Memory and Action Chunk Execution sec:related-memory A single observation may not provide enough information to determine the next action. Memory-based policies address this limitation by retaining information from earlier observations; for example, MemoryVLA stores consolidated perceptual and cognitive entries that can be queried over long horizons shi2026memoryvla . A complementary line of work predicts temporally extended action sequences. ACT introduced transformer-based action chunking to reduce the effective decision horizon zhao2023act , while generative policies such as Diffusion Policy, RDT-1B, and generate multi-step actions with diffusion or flow-based objectives chi2025diffusion,liu2025rdt,black2024pi0 . Such temporal coherence can reduce responsiveness when new observations arrive during execution liu2025bidirectional,zeng2026revisiting . Bidirectional Decoding improves closed-loop adaptation by selecting among candidate chunks liu2025bidirectional , while Consistency Policy and Streaming Diffusion Policy accelerate generative action synthesis prasad2024consistency,hoeg2025streaming . Real-time chunking instead explicitly accounts for inference latency when transitioning between successive chunks black2026real . addresses a complementary setting: it retains visual history across policy updates and uses high-rate tactile feedback to revise the unexecuted portion of an active action chunk. Tactile Foundation Models sec:related-tactile Tactile representation learning aims to produce features that transfer across sensors and tasks bi2026vla, tao2026foretac, heng2025vitacformer, zhang2026tacvla, huang2025tactile . Heterogeneous Tactile Transformer learns a shared model across sensor types bi2026heterogeneous , while FG-CLTP aligns tactile features with visual and language representations ma2026fg . Other work explores transferring representations learned from human tactile recordings to dexterous robots zhang2026human and scaling pretraining through tactile foundation models team2026n0,zhou2026touchworld . Our tactile encoder follows this direction through contrastive pretraining on synchronized tactile and hand-pose histories. Building on tactile representations, several systems study how to incorporate touch into manipulation policies. Multi-rate architectures allow tactile feedback to influence control between visual updates. T-Rex assigns vision and touch to experts operating at different rates niu2026t , while Reactive Diffusion Policy combines a slow visual diffusion policy with a fast latent tactile controller xue2025reactive . FA-RDP adapts this division to task demand zhuo2026fa , and DSWAM organizes world--action modeling into cooperating slow and fast systems zhu2026dswam . Residual adaptation provides another mechanism for incorporating touch into existing policies. ViTaR attaches a lightweight visuotactile residual branch to a frozen backbone wang2026vitar , while ResTacVLA applies residual adaptation in feature space zhang2026feeling . Tactile feedback can also guide action execution through inference-time adaptation. FBFM introduces asynchronous feedback during flow-matching execution without additional training li2026fbfm , while inference-time policy steering adjusts a fixed policy using vision and touch wu2026inference . Complementary approaches use touch as training supervision without requiring tactile input at deployment gubernatorov2026hapticvla,cheng2026tau . These approaches enable tactile feedback to influence action generation and execution. In , a cached, history-aware visual representation connects a slow visual policy to a fast tactile editor, which combines visual memory with recent touch to refine the ongoing action chunk. Predictive supervision encourages these representations to capture evolving interaction dynamics, while auxiliary predictors are used only during training and add no inference cost. Methodology sec:method Overview sec:method-overview During contact-rich manipulation, high frequency changes in contact pressure or location may require the robot to adjust its motion before the next visual update. Tactile feedback captures these local changes, but deciding how to respond also depends on the task instruction and visual information about the ongoing interaction. To retain this information between visual updates, shares a history-aware visual memory between a visual policy and a lightweight tactile editor. The editor combines this cached memory with recent tactile observations to asynchronously correct the remaining actions planned by the visual policy, avoiding the computational cost of rerunning the visual branch. title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
comment: Matthew Strong and Ankush K. Dhawan contributed equally. Project page: https://real2sem2real.github.io/
summary: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.

Introduction End-to-end robot learning maps pixels to actions in closed loop and is a promising route for robots that take on everyday tasks~ kim2024openvla , but it is data hungry. Vision-language-action (VLA) models are pretrained on more than a million robot trajectories~ openx , and Diffusion Policy~ diffusionpolicy still needs on the order of a hundred demonstrations per task. Robot data has two costs -- every trajectory requires human time, and every new object instance requires data collection on that instance, so hundreds of demonstrations of a single object will not generalize to other objects of the same type. Teleoperation~ zhao2023act is physically grounded but difficult to scale, and each alternative does not address every flaw. Demonstration augmentation~ mimicgen, demogen still starts from some teleoperation and needs privileged state or accurate 3D observations. Simulated collection~ robocasa needs modeled assets and a human in the loop, and handheld grippers~ chi2024umi require custom hardware and hundreds of demonstrations per task. Human video~ wang2023mimicplay, kareer2024egomimic, qiu2025hat must first be annotated with states and actions, which requires motion-capture and depth hardware~ wang2024dexcap or for rendering the robot into inpainted 2D frames~ phantom , where objects cannot be moved from their motion in video. Imprecise recovered object motion compounds into drifting poses and implausible geometry (Fig.~ fig:failure_modes ) that are insufficient for a source of data. Real-to-sim-to-real pipelines reconstruct real objects, recover their motion from a video, and render robot demonstrations in simulation with no robot in the loop. Real2Render2Real (R2R2R)~ r2r2r showed that one smartphone scan and one RGB video suffice to fine-tune a VLA, but it augments spatially, not semantically. For example, their exact mug and coffee machine in a human demonstration must be present at deployment, and covering more objects means a scan and a demonstration for every pairing. Digital cousins~ acdc, simfoundry substitute similar simulated assets, but overall similarity does not say where a mug should rest on a new coffee machine. Humans know a mug is lifted by its handle and set on a platform. Given one human video of a mug placed on a coffee machine, why can't a policy succeed on mugs and coffee machines it has never seen? The first step is recovering object trajectories. The strongest pose estimators assume a depth sensor~ foundationpose , and RGB-only trackers drift or fail at initialization on textureless objects. We track each object with a DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splat~ dinov3, 3dgs , optimizing its pose against feature, photometric, silhouette, and monocular depth-ranking losses from an initialization seeded on the table plane. The grasp comes from the demonstrator's hand via HaMeR~ hamer , following the method in Phantom~ phantom . The second step is augmentation. Beyond perturbing object poses, we add semantic and functional augmentation. Cousins are generated with MV-SAM3D~ mvsam3d from one or several images (online, AI-generated, or real photos), and distilled with DINOv3 features. A semantic alignment registers each cousin to the demonstrated object, and for functional placement/motion, a weighted alignment registers each functional and target object by its region of interaction rather than its whole body, so augmentation extends beyond single-object pick-and-place. Finally, an interactive viewer can be employed to build the simulated scene, a camera optimization matches the simulated camera to the real one without AprilTags, and parallel generation in photorealistic IsaacSim~ isaaclab , or MuJoCo~ mujoco , generates over 2 , 000 episodes in about two hours, after about 25 minutes of setup, with no human in the loop. Among prior methods (Table~ tab:taxonomy ), ours is the only one that transfers demonstrations across object instances from a single monocular RGB video. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), summarized in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Our contributions are: . An RGB-only 4D object tracker on DINO-distilled Gaussian splats that outperforms prior methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth; A semantic alignment of digital cousins for whole objects and functional placement/motion regions, producing demonstrations for every cousin pairing; Fast, parallel generation in MuJoCo or IsaacSim, enabled by an interactive scene creation tool that ports directly to simulation; and Nearly 2 , 000 real rollouts on two robots, where a VLA trained on data from one human video per task matches or outperforms two hours of teleoperation. Related Work sec:related-work Learning from human video. The embodiment gap must be closed before human video can supervise a policy. DexCap~ wang2024dexcap uses motion-capture gloves and a depth camera, egocentric methods co-train with robot data~ wang2023mimicplay, kareer2024egomimic, qiu2025hat , and Phantom~ phantom overlays a rendered robot on the 2D video, tying each demonstration to its exact viewpoint and scene. VideoManip~ videomanip , VidAct~ vidact , and WARPED~ warped need less hardware but generate data only for the demonstrated objects in question, lacking generalization. WARPED builds a digital twin of the single object demonstrated per task and augments each demonstration tenfold, retexturing and translating the object, scaling the scene, and perturbing the camera, but never changes the object's shape or geometry. Learning from human video also requires many demonstrations per task, 250 to 350 videos for Phantom and 30 for WARPED (Table~ tab:taxonomy ), whereas R2Sem2R starts from one. Object pose tracking. BundleSDF~ bundlesdf and FoundationPose~ foundationpose track novel objects from RGB-D, so monocular pipelines substitute estimated depth, as VideoManip~ videomanip and VidAct~ vidact do with MoGe-2~ moge2 and MoGe-3~ moge3 , and accuracy hinges on that estimate (Sec.~ sec:tracking-results ). RGB-only alternatives traditionally fit a differentiable renderer. RSRD~ rsrd renders distilled DINO features and fails on textureless objects in our experiments, and WARPED~ warped tracks a splat fitted to a SAM3D-generated mesh from a MegaPose~ megapose initialization, so its errors start from a generated model. We track a splat distilled from a scan of the real object, initialized upright on the table plane. Demonstration generation. MimicGen~ mimicgen , RoboCasa~ robocasa , and DemoGen~ demogen multiply teleoperated demonstrations but need privileged state or depth, or some initial teleoperation. R2R2R~ r2r2r removes both by tracking objects in RGB video and replaying them kinematically, and its followers~ r2rgen, real2edit2real, gaussianfactory, robosimgs widen spatial augmentation. All vary where the demonstrated objects are, not which. Digital cousins and category-level generation. ACDC~ acdc introduced digital cousins, and SimFoundry~ simfoundry , WorldComposer~ worldcomposer , and RoboCousin~ robocousin build sim-ready scenes and cousins from video, panoramas, or images, but take their trajectories from teleoperation, scripted skills, or planners, and SimFoundry registers cousins by overall geometry, which does not compute where a placed object must rest. Vision-language agents convert a recording into a simulatable twin~ agenticreal2sim , but each conversion often runs up to an hour per scene and reproduces only one scene in non-modular fashion. However, some methods transfer a demonstration across instances. Real2Gen~ real2gen uses two RGB-D cameras and places the object at the center of the target, which does not extend to a tray or a peg. ShapeGen~ shapegen collects five teleoperated RGB-D demonstrations per task, annotates contacts and keypoints, and trains a shape warping, changing only the manipulated object. AffordGen~ affordgen transfers annotated keypoints with DINOv2 under the same assumptions. R2Sem2R removes each requirement. It starts from one monocular RGB human video with no teleoperation, annotation, or trained warping, and also varies the target object, in addition to the grasped object. Distilled feature fields~ f3rm, rsrd have helped with retrieval, segmentation, and grasp transfer, and we use DINOv3 features~ dinov3 , distilled into each cousin's splat, to align whole objects and the contact region from the human demonstration autonomously (Sec.~ sec:align ). Method sec:method R2Sem2R takes one RGB video of a human performing the task, a phone scan of the demonstrated objects, and photographs of cousin objects. With one demonstration, object trajectories and valid grasps in the object's frame are computed, and we can use inverse kinematics (Sec.~ sec:ik ) for any manipulator with a parallel-jaw gripper. title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
comment: Accepted at Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.

Introduction In recent years, imitation learning from human demonstrations has become a dominant method for advanced learning-based control of robots. This is particularly the case in the field of manipulation chi2023diffusionpolicy, chi2024diffusionpolicy,Ze2024DP3 and locomotion 2018-TOG-deepMimic, manilocsurvey . Conversely, for aerial vehicle autonomy, imitation learning from human demonstrations has not experienced comparable widespread adoption. In the case of quadrotors, in particular, two major trends have been imitation learning from (privileged) expert policies loquercio_2021_learning_high_speed_flight_in_the_wild,kaufmann2020RSS,eschmann_2026_raptor and using pre-trained models as vision encoders saviolo2025nova,xing2024bootstrapping . The latter promise to bring broader generalization by virtue of having been pre-trained on massive amounts of real-world images collected from the internet. Imitation learning from human demonstrations and pre-trained vision models are motivated and driven by scaling laws that were first observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) kaplan2020scaling . Early indications hint that similar scaling laws might exist in robot imitation learning lin2024data . The potential that scaling robot imitation data could bear similarly large returns as LLM scaling, has led to the formation of a large number of commercial robot imitation data creation/curation companies. These companies also bet on monopolizing forces known as the ``data flywheels'' grannen2025robot limiting accessibility while the capital expenditure (CAPEX) requirement for large-scale robot data collection is by itself already a major hurdle for reproducibility and progress in the community. The alternative is training robot control policies entirely in simulation without requiring real-world data. Not only are methods fully trained on synthetic data more accessible to fellow researchers, but they are also more introspectable. Due to the lack of interpretability of deep neural networks, in general we cannot get strong guarantees for learned end-to-end controllers. The best way to reason about the behavior of the trained control policy is through introspection of the data that went into training it. For vision foundation models dosovitskiy2021an, radford2021learning, simeoni2025dinov3, carion2025sam3segmentconcepts this data is usually proprietary, hampering reproducibility, interpretability of the resulting behavior and the opportunity for independent researchers to study effects of modifying the data distribution. To accelerate the research of vision-based aerial vehicle control we present the following contributions: HyperDrone: An extremely fast simulator for training end-to-end visual control policies. HyperDrone consists of: HyperLux: A fast, large-batch ray-tracing renderer for RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow perception Highly optimized multirotor dynamics simulation Sim2Real Transfer of a yaw-control policy trained entirely in simulation Related Work sec:related-work In the recent past, several quadrotor simulators have been proposed and optimized for different purposes. We focus on simulating cameras and quadrotor dynamics to support visual control policies, and the main related simulators are listed in Table tab:simulator_comparison . A very popular simulator for this purpose has been Flightmare song2020flightmare . However, it does not support batch rendering and hence is comparatively slow. It has been measured to yield Frames Per Second (FPS) in li2025visfly which is prohibitively slow for reinforcement learning which usually requires millions or even billions of samples. Furthermore, it requires proprietary, licensed software to replace the default scenes. To overcome the low rendering throughput, multiple batch-rendering-based simulators have been proposed. These cluster into Nvidia Isaac-based and Habitat-based simulators. VisFly li2025visfly is based on a custom version of Habitat habitat19iccv for batch rendering. Habitat in turn uses OpenGL through the Magnum engine. It is the only other simulator that supports quadrotor dynamics, batch rendering and is compatible with the latest generation GPUs (Nvidia Blackwell/5000-series, released in early 2025). However, it falls short of HyperDrone when it comes to fidelity features like motion blur and anti-aliasing. Note that we leave an exhaustive performance comparison for later and only focus on qualitative features in this section. Aerial Gym kulkarni2025aerial is based on Isaac Gym and implements a batch raytracer mainly for depth perception and semantic segmentation. While depth perception and semantic segmentation is also supported in HyperDrone, our main focus is on RGB observations which are not supported for general 3D mesh scenes (only for simple geometric objects) by Aerial Gym. Furthermore, due to Nvidia Warp limitations, Aerial Gym does not take advantage of ray-tracing cores in modern GPUs. Additionally, Isaac Gym, which Aerial Gym builds upon, was deprecated in mid-2024 and hence Aerial Gym does not support Nvidia Blackwell GPUs (5000 series). OmniDrones xu2024omnidrones follows a similar strategy by building onto Isaac Sim. Compared to Aerial Gym it does not implement its own rendering pipeline and relies on Isaac Sim for camera simulation. OmniDrones is built on Isaac Sim 4.1.0 which was released in mid-2024 and hence does not support Blackwell/5000-series GPUs, either. Since the project is not maintained anymore we do not expect this to change. Initially, when conceptualizing HyperDrone we were planning to build it on top of Madrona rosenzweig2024madrona , an open-source batch raytracer and rasterizer that has shown promising performance. However, while investigating Madrona we found that it does not take advantage of ray-tracing hardware in RTX-series cards and that the codebase is relatively complex. Hence, we concluded that there is a need for a new simulator that focuses on rendering performance while supporting the needs of realistic visual quadrotor simulation like motion blur, anti-aliasing and reflections. While designing HyperDrone we also keep in mind that in the future we should support rolling-shutter simulation as well, even though for now we focus on global shutter cameras. Method In the following we describe the architecture of HyperDrone and then the control problem formulation, platform and general setup for the simulation-to-reality transfer of a visual policy trained from scratch in HyperDrone. Architecture A main premise guiding the architecture of HyperDrone is that we want to avoid CPU GPU memory transfers that commonly occur when quadrotor dynamics simulation is being run on the CPU while a batch renderer is run on the GPU. With OptiX, both run on the GPU. Another premise motivated in Section sec:related-work is the ability to take advantage of the ray-tracing cores in modern hardware. The first component of HyperDrone is HyperLux, our ray-tracing renderer. Ray-tracing cores are fixed-function hardware that accelerate finding intersections of 3D rays with a 3D mesh. Compared to rasterization, which maps 3D geometry from a 3D mesh onto the camera plane, ray-tracing takes the more physically motivated approach of tracing rays of light. In practice, we shoot a ray from each pixel towards the 3D mesh and find the first point of intersection (this is what the ray-tracing fixed-function hardware supports). Once we identify the intersection, we can use the information from the mesh to e.g. look up the appropriate color for that particular intersection point from a texture map. To make this tractable the 3D mesh first needs to be processed into an accelerated data-structure. This acceleration structure and using ray-tracing cores to intersect rays with it is not accessible via compute APIs like CUDA. HyperLux therefore uses Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan or Apple Metal, which handle the acceleration structure and return intersection points for the rays we supply, and falls back to software ray traversal on WebGPU, which does not expose ray-tracing hardware. The second component of HyperDrone is the quadrotor dynamics simulator. The quadrotor dynamics simulation is based on the implementation introduced in eschmann2024learningtofly combined with years of continuous development, refactoring and improvements. Due to rendering not being the bottleneck anymore (cf. rendering performance benchmarks in Section sec:results ), we can just render every frame from scratch. This basically rules out overfitting to any particular dataset in the traditional sense. We might still overfit to the data-distribution that the simulator generates (e.g. in terms of visual fidelity, artifacts etc.) but overfitting to particular samples is virtually ruled out by never using a sample twice. For the proof-of-concept of the simulation-to-reality transfer, we use RAPTOR eschmann_2026_raptor as a teacher policy and train a student policy to estimate the yaw between a target frame and the current frame (more in the next Section sec:sim2real ). We run both the teacher and the student on the GPU as well. Please refer to Figure~ fig:gpu for a graphical overview of the HyperDrone architecture. We choose a simple task to disentangle the visual simulation-to-reality transfer from control challenges. As can be seen in Figure fig:experimental-setup , we abstract most of the high-frequency control problem by using the RAPTOR eschmann_2026_raptor foundation policy for low-level and position control and only leave yaw control to the network trained in simulation and deployed on a real camera. The task of the student policy is to provide the relative yaw offset between a target frame and the current frame. Hence, we use a convolutional network on the channel-wise stack of both frames, followed by a dense head that predicts the relative yaw. We want to support a large diversity of 3D scenes to avoid overfitting to a specific scene. Hence, we use the procedurally generated indoor scenes from the ProcTHOR procthor dataset. This dataset includes diverse indoor scenes with randomized room layouts and object placements (cf. Figure fig:procthor ). It also strikes a good balance between realism and performance (cf. title: SimPT: An Automated Simulation Framework for Intervention-Based VLA Post-Training
summary: Human-in-the-loop (HIL) post-training improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through expert corrections, but costly human supervision and repeated real-robot evaluation limit algorithm exploration and development. We introduce SimPT (Simulation-based Post-Training), a simulation framework that automates intervention-based VLA post-training by integrating policy rollouts, corrective data collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation. To automatically determine intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots during policy execution. After a rollout fails, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from these snapshots, starting at more advanced task stages and falling back to earlier ones as needed to generate corrective trajectories. We implement and compare four post-training methods, RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO, across seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Relative to a fixed-interval snapshot baseline, the Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts by 75.0% and increases recovery success from 93.4% to 98.9%. Using SimPT, we develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines cross-fitting and low-pass filtering of value predictions. This refinement increases the overall success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials. In real-robot HIL post-training, it increases the success rate from 72% to 96% across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task. These results demonstrate the utility of SimPT for exploring and developing VLA post-training algorithms.

Introduction sec:introduction Generalist vision--language--action (VLA) policies map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions black2025pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . When these policies encounter states outside the demonstration distribution, or out-of-distribution (OOD) states, they may produce inappropriate actions laskey2017dart . Such errors can drive the robot further from the demonstration distribution and compound over time~ ross2011dagger . Human-in-the-loop (HIL) robot learning addresses this problem through expert takeover, using corrective demonstrations to update the policy ravichandar2020lfd,kelly2019hgdagger,luo2025hilserl . However, developing HIL algorithms on physical robots requires substantial human effort to collect corrections and repeated hardware use for evaluation. Environmental variation further complicates reproducible comparisons li2025simpler . These costs and sources of variability limit systematic exploration and development of HIL post-training algorithms. Simulation offers controllable scenes, repeatable trials, and scalable data collection for developing and evaluating HIL algorithms before hardware experiments mandlekar2023mimicgen,jiang2025dexmimicgen . Platforms such as RoboTwin mu2025robotwin and SIMPLER li2025simpler support demonstration generation, policy evaluation, and sim-to-real research, while automated HIL post-training remains comparatively underexplored. IntervenGen extends simulation-based data generation to corrective behavior by expanding a small set of human interventions into synthetic recovery trajectories, but relies on human experts to determine when and how to intervene in the initial recovery demonstrations hoque2024intervengen . Automating these decisions in simulation requires selecting suitable recovery states along a failed policy rollout and determining how an expert should complete the task from those states. Both depend on task progress. Vision-language models (VLMs) can monitor execution, but repeated visual queries incur inference overhead guo2024doremi . CuRobo-based scripted experts can execute predefined task sequences from initial states sundaralingam2023curobo , but the motion planner itself does not infer task progress or select corrective actions for states reached by the policy. Motivated by these challenges, we introduce SimPT, a simulation framework that integrates policy rollouts, automated corrective data collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation to support the exploration and development of VLA post-training algorithms (Fig.~ fig:framework ). To guide recovery, an agent compiles task information into an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph. During policy execution, the graph tracks task progress through fixed checks on privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots without further agent queries. After rollout failure, SimPT attempts expert recovery from snapshots at more advanced task stages and falls back to earlier ones as needed. A CuRobo-based expert resumes execution from each restored state, and successful recovery trajectories are retained for policy post-training. Using SimPT, we implement and compare HG-DAgger kelly2019hgdagger , RECAP physicalintelligence2025recap , DPO+SFT rafailov2023dpo , and FlowPRO wu2026flowpro on seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks. In independent data collections, the Progress Graph requires 75.0 fewer recovery attempts than a fixed-interval snapshot baseline. We further use SimPT to develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines cross-fitting (CF) and Butterworth low-pass filtering (LPF) of value predictions. This combined refinement increases the overall success rate from 76.50 to 79.36 in held-out simulation trials. Applied to real-robot HIL post-training, it increases success from 72 to 96 across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task. We develop the Agent-Compiled Progress Graph to track task progress and retain stable snapshots during policy execution. After rollout failure, expert recovery starts from more advanced task stages and falls back to earlier ones as needed. We compare four post-training methods on seven RoboTwin tasks and use SimPT to develop RECAP-CF-LPF. By combining cross-fitting and low-pass filtering, this refinement improves policy success in both simulation and real-robot HIL post-training. Related Work sec:related_work Intervention-Based Robot Learning Interactive imitation learning mitigates distribution shift by collecting expert supervision during policy execution zhang2017safedagger . DAgger aggregates expert labels on states encountered by the learner and retrains the policy on the expanded dataset ross2011dagger . HIL variants differ in how they allocate expert control: HG-DAgger lets a human expert decide when to take over and return control kelly2019hgdagger , whereas ThriftyDAgger requests assistance based on novelty and estimated risk within an intervention budget hoque2022thriftydagger . Their behavior-cloning policy updates use expert-labeled data celemin2022iilreview , without directly using the success or failure of autonomous rollouts as learning signals. To learn from autonomous experience as well as expert corrections, recent VLA post-training methods incorporate reinforcement learning (RL) deng2025rlvlasurvey . RECAP learns a value function to estimate future returns, accounting for remaining task steps and failure penalties, and uses the resulting advantages to condition policy training physicalintelligence2025recap . Noisy frame-level value estimates can nevertheless yield misleading advantages in OOD states. STEAM addresses this challenge by learning temporal-offset predictors from frame pairs in expert demonstrations and conservatively combining their advantage estimates liu2026steam . Its ensemble reduces advantage overestimation at the cost of training and evaluating multiple predictors. Preference optimization offers an alternative without a separately trained value function or critic. FlowPRO adapts direct preference optimization (DPO) rafailov2023dpo to flow-matching VLAs and uses a proximal regularizer to constrain implicit reward magnitudes and mitigate reward hacking. Its preference pairs are constructed from failed and corrective trajectories collected through human intervention and rollback wu2026flowpro . Across these approaches, corrective data collection and repeated real-robot evaluation demand substantial expert time and hardware resources, constraining systematic algorithm exploration. Task Monitoring and Failure Recovery Task monitoring connects execution feedback to failure detection and recovery huang2023innermonologue,liu2023reflect . DoReMi uses VLM queries to detect task-constraint violations and trigger replanning guo2024doremi . Language-model agents also encode task knowledge in executable programs for robot planning and control, as demonstrated by Code as Policies liang2023codeaspolicies , ProgPrompt singh2023progprompt , and VoxPoser huang2023voxposer . RoboTwin combines generative digital twins with task code to generate demonstrations and benchmark manipulation policies mu2025robotwin . Related benchmarks study knowledge transfer in lifelong robot learning, as in LIBERO liu2023libero , and unify policy evaluation across simulation and the real world, as in RoboDojo chen2026robodojo . IntervenGen extends data generation to recovery behavior, focusing on robustness to object pose estimation errors. It combines closed-loop policy execution with transformed replay of human source interventions to synthesize corrective trajectories hoque2024intervengen . RLinf provides scalable infrastructure for embodied RL yu2026rlinf , while its real-world extension, USER, supports asynchronous online policy learning. Its HG-DAgger workflow relies on human experts to determine intervention timing and provide corrective actions zang2026user . Method sec:method Framework Overview sec:framework As shown in Fig.~ fig:framework , SimPT uses a Progress Graph to connect policy execution with automated corrective data collection, followed by policy post-training and standalone evaluation. Language-model agents compile task specifications into candidate graphs, which undergo validation and selection. Scripts then calibrate the selected graph's data-dependent thresholds using simulated expert trajectories. During policy execution, the graph tracks task progress and retains stable snapshots. If the rollout ends in failure, a programmatic expert attempts recovery from these snapshots to generate corrective trajectories. title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it. Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold. Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models. In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.

They inherit the representations and rich spatiotemporal knowledge from generative backbones with scalable pretraining, predict the future with world modeling objective, and generate actions from the features from the reasoning process. It has been shown that they improve generalization to out-of-distribution scenes by predicting how the world changes. However, recent researches question whether the capabilities of WAMs come from explicit test-time prediction or enriched representations from the world modeling, and whether video prediction is a good representational prior or objective for world modeling. FastWAM finds that representational gains from world modeling, rather than explicit future generation at test time, is the main contributor of WAM's performance yuan2026fastwam . Furthermore, ImageWAM shows image editors as backbones led to significant improvements to the policy generalization from edit-aware representation which contain task-relevant visual changes and is evidenced by attention maps zhang2026imagewam . We therefore ask: Understanding this question is necessary to explain why some inherited representations support stronger generalization. Inspired by the baseline WAMs and fundamental questions about their representations and performances, we start by analyzing the representational geometry of in- and out-of-distribution observations. Throughout the paper, we introduce nuisance orthogonality, which characterized the geometric separation between feature displacement from visual variations and the empirical in-distribution manifold. High nuisance orthogonality therefore measures a potential for disentangled representational prior which presents in the generative backbones before policy training. We show that nuisance orthogonality is highly related to the generalization performance of WAMs, across visual variations and models, allowing prospective diagnostics of world models. Furthermore, we present nuisance suppression after policy training, a suppressing behavior of residual displacement so that the policy can remove nuisance information, improve scene retrieval, and enable robust action generation. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=1.5em,topsep=1.5pt,itemsep=1.5pt] A geometric characterization of representational priors: Nuisance orthogonality, the fraction of feature displacement orthogonal to the empirical span of in-distribution data, quantifying whether a backbone separates action preserving visual changes from directions that distinguish clean scenes. Related Work sec:related World Action Models. World action models (WAMs) are emerging as a major paradigm for robot foundation models by action generation with predictive modeling of future visual observations kim2026cosmospolicy, ye2026dreamzero, li2026lingbotva, pai2025mimicvideo, nvidia2026cosmos3 . Their appeal lies in transferring spatiotemporal priors from generative pretraining to robotics control, while future prediction provides supervision linking actions to their visual consequences. Empirical studies report improved data efficiency and generalization to unseen objects, tasks, and environments, with strong robustness under visual perturbations zhang2026wamrobustness . Beyond direct policy execution, predictive world modeling can help test-time planning by evaluating the consequences of candidate actions kim2026cosmospolicy,zhou2026tau0wm . Recent work further shows that video prediction co-training is necessary to improve world representation, but explicit test-time generation contributes only to trivial improvements of downstream tasks yuan2026fastwam . These researches motivate examining the representational priors of generative backbones and their underlying generalization performance. Our study investigates which geometric properties inherited from visual pretraining are related with robustness and how they reshape after policy adaptation. Nuisance separation and representation geometry. Nuisance invariance and disentanglement provide a foundation for separating task information from irrelevant variation achille2018invariance , although unsupervised disentanglement is not identifiable without inductive biases or supervision locatello2019challenging . Related objectives remove nuisance factors adversarially ganin2016dann , separate shared from domain-specific features, or encourage orthogonality between task and nuisance representations bousmalis2016dsn,sarhan2020orthogonal , with applications in domain adaptation and fair representation learning. In robot manipulation, prior work has decomposed generalization failures into factors of variation and studied which properties of pretrained visual representations predict robustness to distribution shift xie2024decomposing,pmlr-v270-burns25a . In visual reinforcement learning, similar ideas enable transfer across visual domains and robustness to task-irrelevant distractors higgins2017darla,zhang2021dbc . More recent work disentangles nuisance factors through explicit or implicit separation in latent action pretraining bu2025univla,li2025latbot,jeong2026vila,dai2026conla,zhang2026dila . Our diagnostic instead measures nuisance separation in pretrained representations and relates it empirically to policy robustness. title: NavBind: Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history. We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history. We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.

Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history. Introduction sec:introduction In vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) krantz2020beyond , vision-language-action (VLA) models zhang2024navid map visual observations and instructions to actions. Success rate measures whether an agent reaches the goal but does not establish whether it follows the instruction. Route-fidelity metrics jain-etal-2019-stay assess the similarity between the generated trajectory and the ground-truth trajectory, providing an indirect measure of instruction following. However, these metrics still cannot establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions, as it may instead rely on visual cues or navigation history alone. Language interventions, i.e., changing the language instruction and observing how the local actions or navigation performance change, provide a more direct test of language dependence. NavTrust jiang2026navtrust and Contrast Sets anwar2025contrast rephrase instructions and assess changes in navigation performance. However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged. R2RIE-CE taioli2024mind modifies instructions by injecting direction, object, and room errors. However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them. Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them. We therefore ask not merely whether the model's behaviour changes, but whether changing the instruction to describe another feasible route makes the model more likely to choose the corresponding actions. We keep the agent's state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix fixed. In Figure~ fig:overview , both turning left and continuing up the stairs are feasible, and the remaining instruction specifies which branch to take. We use instruction-action binding to describe the requirement that the model assigns higher probability to the actions required by the instruction. We introduce , a controlled diagnostic built through cross-route recombination of route-instruction examples drawn from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Using fine-grained route-language alignments, we retain one example's completed instruction prefix and combine it with either its original suffix or a compatible suffix from another route. The resulting full-instruction pairs specify different executable branches under the same replayed history and agent state, yielding 3,252 contexts with reference action sequences for both branches. Within each fixed context, we first ask: does changing the instruction change the action sequence the model generates? We then ask: does the model assign higher probability to the actions for a branch when instructed to take that branch rather than the other? We test this by comparing the likelihood of each reference action sequence under the two instructions. This comparison can reveal changes in action preference even when the generated sequence stays the same. Finally, we examine the visual response: do attention heatmaps and gradient-based attribution heatmaps highlight different image regions under the two instructions? We evaluate four navigation VLAs on : Uni-NaVid zhang2025uninavid , StreamVLN wei2025streamvln , JanusVLN zeng2026janusvln , and FutureNav zhang2026futurenav . We find that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. (Table~ tab:main-results ). It also shows that models respond more strongly when the instructions contrast opposite turns than when they contrast forward movement with a turn. Our contributions are: We construct by recombining instruction segments across routes into full instructions for two feasible branches. Each pair preserves the agent state, history, and completed instruction prefix, and provides reference action sequences for both branches. We diagnose instruction-action binding using generated sequences to measure output changes, fixed-target likelihoods to assess preferences for the instructed actions, and attention and gradient-based attribution heatmaps to track spatial changes. We show that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. This supports evaluating how language affects local decisions alongside navigation success. Related Work sec:related-work Language Diagnostics in VLN Instruction fidelity beyond success. Goal completion can obscure whether an agent followed the described route. Stay on the Path introduced CLS and longer R4R routes jain-etal-2019-stay , while LAW extended language-aligned supervision and evaluation to VLN-CE raychaudhuri-etal-2021-language . Modality ablations further showed that R2R agents could rely strongly on graph structure hu-etal-2019-looking . These works motivate language-specific evaluation through task metrics, supervision, and modality ablations. Language interventions in VLN. Early diagnostics mask object, direction, and numerical cues zhu-etal-2022-diagnosing and swap directional tokens hahn2023which . Skill-focused evaluations append atomic instructions to truncated RxR episodes yang2023behavioral and construct human-refined atomic instructions, including same-start left/right pairs wang-etal-2024-navigating . These studies evaluate agents on discrete navigation graphs and their action tests cannot be directly applied to navigation VLAs that execute low-level actions. In VLN-CE, NavTrust evaluates whether agents maintain navigation performance under instruction corruption and stylistic variation jiang2026navtrust . Contrast Sets tests instruction rephrasing with unchanged navigation goals on a physical robot anwar2025contrast . However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged. R2RIE-CE injects direction, object, and room errors into instructions to study error detection and localization taioli2024mind . title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
summary: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.

Given an observation and a language instruction , the backbone produces a compact world prior . TIDE turns these deployment-time states into training signals within the same session. The client executes actions from either the policy or the human operator and streams executed-action records to the server. The server handles policy inference, stores the incoming records, and makes them available to the learner. The learner updates all trainable policy modules online and returns new policy checkpoints at episode boundaries. Robot client The robot client is responsible for low-latency real-robot control. At each control step, it collects observations, requests action chunks from the server, and executes policy actions unless the operator intervenes. Inspired by RTC~ black2025real,black2025training , the client adopts asynchronous real-time chunking: committed actions continue to execute while future actions are refreshed in the background. This design reduces inference-induced stalls and smooths transitions between consecutive action chunks. During takeover, VR delta control allows the operator to command incremental motions around the current robot state and return control to the policy without resetting the episode. Each handoff clears queued policy chunks to prevent stale actions from being executed. The client streams executed actions and intervention flags asynchronously to the server, keeping data recording off the critical control path. It centralizes GPU-based policy inference and writes online episodes to a shared dataset, while leaving low-latency control to the robot client. For each client query, the server runs the active checkpoint on the current observation and returns an action chunk. In parallel, it appends execution records and manages episode commit or discard. At episode end, the human operator manually confirms task completion. Before upload, the server commits only confirmed-successful episodes; failed, timed-out, aborted or stopped, reset-before-completion, re-recorded, stale, and unrecovered episodes are discarded. To ensure rollout consistency, the server adopts learner-produced checkpoints only at episode boundaries, so that each rollout is associated with a single policy generation. As committed records arrive, it reads from the growing online dataset and jointly updates the video diffusion backbone, cross-modal adapter/Q-former, action expert, and source embeddings with offline task data; the pretrained text encoder and video VAE remain frozen. The learner allocates 0.2 optimizer steps per newly committed control frame and publishes a checkpoint every five committed episodes. The server prefetches new weights and adopts them only at the next episode boundary. This mechanism returns model improvements to the robot during deployment while ensuring that each rollout is generated by a single policy generation. Human-executed chunks provide supervision for failure recovery and difficult states, while policy-executed chunks provide additional learning signal from behaviors that the current policy can already perform. Chunk-level provenance labels allow TIDE to use both sources of deployment data without flattening mixed episodes into homogeneous expert demonstrations. title: Relational Geometry Forcing for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions. However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation. Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models. Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features. To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features. Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.

Introduction sec:introduction Robot policies for manipulation require accounting for interaction-induced scene changes when generating precise action trajectories. World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate predictive world modeling into action learning by coupling future visual prediction with action generation~ dreamzero,lingbotva,cosmospolicy,bi2026motus . Typically, WAMs include a video expert to predict future RGB frames and an action expert to generate action chunks, while scene geometry receives no direct supervision~ yuan2026fastwam,gigaworldpolicy . Accordingly, limited geometric perception of the physical scene remains a key challenge for WAMs in precise manipulation~ shridhar2022peract,ze2024dp3 . Recent geometry-aware WAMs address this challenge by adding explicit geometry branches to the video--action framework, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (a). These branches introduce depth or 4D prediction as additional training objectives~ guo2026xwam,ma2026geosemwam,li2026wam4d,zhang2026mecowam . We therefore ask whether geometric priors can directly regularize the video and action representations of WAMs without explicit geometric reconstruction. Representation alignment offers an alternative to explicit geometric modeling by directly supervising intermediate WAM features. REPA aligns diffusion features with pretrained visual representations~ yu2025repa , while subsequent methods use geometric targets from pretrained 3D foundation models to supervise video generators and robot policies~ wu2026geometry,li2026spatial . As illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (b), these methods primarily use pointwise alignment to regress intermediate features in WAMs toward dense geometric targets from 3D foundation models. However, pointwise alignment assumes that each WAM feature and its geometric target encode comparable content. Video alignment satisfies this assumption because both representations describe local image regions. In action alignment, compact action features instead summarize trajectory transitions, whereas dense geometric targets describe scene content. Directly regressing action features toward scene-level geometric targets therefore conflates representations with different roles. Consistent with this analysis, extending pointwise alignment to the action expert reduces task success below the unaligned baseline (Figure~ fig:teaser-result b). To address this problem, we introduce ( ), which transfers geometric priors to WAM features without explicit geometric reconstruction. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (c), aligns pairwise relations among WAM features with those induced by a frozen 3D foundation model, avoiding direct feature regression. Matching these relations does not require WAM and 3D features to share the same dimensionality or embedding space~ park2019rkd,zhang2025videorepa . Using frozen VGGT features as supervision~ wang2025vggt , transfers scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to video features through intra-frame and cross-view objectives, while its action-temporal objective couples action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. All auxiliary components are used only during training, leaving inference unchanged. Experiments on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , and real-world tasks on a Franka robot show that achieves competitive performance across single-arm and bimanual manipulation. On the real robot, further generalizes to unseen objects, background distractors, and height changes. Moreover, yields consistent gains across diverse WAM paradigms. Qualitatively, Figure~ fig:teaser-result (a) shows that the similarity map peaks near the ground-truth cross-view correspondence. Our contributions are as follows: We identify a representation mismatch in pointwise alignment between dense geometric targets from 3D foundation models and compact action features in WAMs, explaining the performance degradation observed when this alignment is extended to the action expert. We propose , which transfers geometric priors into WAM representations by aligning intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations, without explicit geometric reconstruction or additional inference modules. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world tasks validate , demonstrating competitive performance, generalization to unseen real-world conditions, and consistent gains across WAM paradigms. Early generative policies use predicted frames or visual plans to guide action generation~ unipi,gr1,vpp , while recent video-action models adapt large-scale video priors through zero-shot, inverse-dynamics, causal, or action-centered formulations~ dreamzero,mimicvideo,lingbotva,bi2026motus,cosmospolicy,gigaworldpolicy . Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam shows that video co-training can improve action learning without inference-time future generation. X-WAM generates multi-view RGB-D sequences~ guo2026xwam , whereas GeoSem-WAM and WAM4D introduce auxiliary depth prediction~ ma2026geosemwam,li2026wam4d . MECo-WAM adds a training-time 4D expert~ zhang2026mecowam . Unlike these methods, regularizes video--action representations through pairwise feature relations without training a depth or 4D predictor. Representation Alignment. Aligning intermediate features with frozen foundation models transfers visual and geometric priors to downstream models~ yan2026svam,wang2026vega . title: Plan First, Act Later: Streaming Reasoning for Executable Memory in Robot Control
summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}. A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%. In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%). These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/

Code and videos can be found on our website: INTRODUCTION Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made substantial progress toward general-purpose robot control intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld, kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel . By grounding language instructions in visual observations and actions, VLA provides a flexible interface for solving diverse manipulation tasks in generalizable open-world. However, many existing policies still rely on a Markovian or near-Markovian view of the world: the action to execute is assumed to be recoverable from the current observation or a short window of recent frames. This assumption becomes fragile in memory-dependent settings, where successful behavior may depend on historical information observed much earlier. For example, repetitive manipulation requires remembering progress yang2026eventvlaeventdrivenvisualevidence,dai2026robommebenchmarkingunderstandingmemory,chen2026rmbenchmemorydependentroboticmanipulation and active exploration requires retrieving the location or state of an object discovered earlier when the robot revisits the scene shah2026memoryretrievalvisuomotorpolicies,sridhar2025memerscalingmemoryrobot . To address these memory-dependent challenges, recent works augment VLA models with a memory bank that retains task-relevant information from past observations. At execution time, the model retrieves relevant entries from the bank to support stable long-term decision making torne2026memmultiscaleembodiedmemory,sridhar2025memerscalingmemoryrobot, shi2026memoryvlaperceptualcognitivememoryvisionlanguageaction . Although this avoids repeatedly processing the raw history, the high-level model must still search across a large memory bank and infer the next subtask at inference time. Such banks often contain redundant information, making it difficult for the model to fetch the required information and lead to more task failures. One key observation is that: As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:main-overview , the task requires the robot to press the button and then pick up the highlighted cube. While the robot is still pressing the button, the model can store the future subtask ``pick up the cube'' in the subtask list when the cube is highlighted. When the transient highlight disappears, the robot can simply retrieve the stored subtask for execution, without re-identifying which cube to pick up. This pattern occurs in many memory-dependent robotic tasks, where the future plan can be determined once the necessary evidence becomes available. Motivated by this view, we propose Plan First, Act Later ( ), a hierarchical memory pipeline for VLA long-term decision-making. It comprises a three-level memory system: a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable subtask list. These three memory components have distinct roles: the visual buffer retains recent observations, the semantic-event memory maintains task-relevant events, and the executable subtask list stores future-relevant subtasks text instructions. At each query, a high-level vision-language model (VLM) updates the event memory and the subtask list, then selects the subtask to execute for the low-level VLA. This design has two benefits: (1) first, streaming memory updates incrementally compress the visual history, reducing the context required for long-horizon reasoning; (2) second, the stored subtasks can be directly retrieved without searching across a large memory bank for subtask inference. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we propose a two-stage training pipeline. The pipeline combines dense update-timing supervision with self-labeling and a task-grounded verifier, allowing the training data to better reflect the model's execution rollout distribution. Evaluation results on RoboMME dai2026robommebenchmarkingunderstandingmemory , a benchmark of long-horizon, memory-dependent manipulation tasks, show that achieves a 56.05 success rate, compared with 44.51 for the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul. In real-world manipulation experiments across four tasks, reaches 60.83 overall success, outperforming MemER (45.00 ) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33 ), demonstrating the practical benefits of our approach. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=1em, labelsep=0.3em, topsep=0pt, itemsep=2pt] We introduce , a hierarchical memory architecture with a streaming-style reasoning mechanism for VLA long-term decision-making. It progressively transforms streaming visual observations into semantic events and executable subtasks, providing a structured memory for diverse long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. We develop a two-stage training pipeline that enables the model to learn reliable hierarchical-memory update behavior. It produces accurate and timely memory updates, yielding reliable executable subtask lists for long-horizon reasoning. title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.

On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38 overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38 without self-evolution.
