Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, providing a foundation for general-purpose manipulation~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . Long-horizon tasks, however, can require information that the current observation does not reveal~ koo2025hamlet,dai2026robomme . For example, when a robot must repeat an operation a specified number of times, similar images may call for different decisions depending on how many repetitions have actually succeeded. An earlier observation may also contain a cue that is no longer visible. Such history-dependent decisions require preserving task-relevant information and tracking execution outcomes over successive interactions. Existing research provides several foundations for these capabilities. Memory-augmented policies equip VLA models with mechanisms for retaining and using historical information, including compact temporal representations koo2025hamlet,jang2025contextvla,zhu2026weavela , memory retrieval, and recurrent state updates~ shi2025memoryvla,hu2026echo,li2026rememvla . Hierarchical architectures introduce a high-level planning layer that issues intermediate decisions to low-level executors ahn2022saycan,belkhale2024rth,duan2025robopara,sridhar2025memer and can incorporate environment feedback~ huang2022innermonologue . Agentic systems further organize reasoning, actions, and feedback into iterative decision processes yao2023react,shinn2023reflexion,wang2024voyager . Recent embodied harnesses explore external task management~ zhang2026harnessvla,gu2026harnesswam and experience-driven adaptation chen2026eta,wang2026shaper,ding2026zetta . Together, these developments motivate studying how the high-level planner in a hierarchical architecture can manage task context and make use of execution experience. Our focus is on two connected responsibilities of this planning process. Within an episode, issuing a command does not establish that the intended operation has succeeded. In the repetition example, updating progress requires interpreting subsequent observations and feedback, while retaining information needed for later decisions. Access to history therefore needs to be accompanied by an explicit process for maintaining decision-relevant task context. Across attempts, an execution record must be translated into a reusable change to influence future planning. This raises a question: how can we support both ongoing context management and improvements to the planning process from execution experience? We explore an editable harness around the high-level VLM as a common mechanism for these responsibilities. The harness organizes context and feedback during execution, while providing an explicit object for revision during self-evolution. This also offers a way to investigate experience reuse when additional demonstrations and manual annotations are costly. Figure~ fig:motivation illustrates this design direction. We present SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent) , which organizes a VLM as an agent within an editable harness around a fixed VLA executor. During task execution, the harness supports sustained context management over long horizons, guiding the extraction, retention, and updating of task progress and execution outcomes from observations and feedback. This context supports the VLM's subsequent planning. However, a predefined harness may not anticipate all task requirements, motivating execution-driven self-evolution to identify and repair its limitations. Analysis and revision agents autonomously diagnose failures from execution traces and propose candidate repairs to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and control rules. A verifier evaluates these candidates through environment rollouts, providing feedback for further revision and harness selection. This process revises the harness without manually constructing additional demonstration datasets for supervised fine-tuning of the high-level VLM planner. The selected harness is fixed before held-out testing, while task context continues to be updated within each episode. We evaluate SERA on RoboMME, a benchmark for history-dependent robotic manipulation~ dai2026robomme . Autonomous SERA achieves 51.38 overall success, compared with 44.38 without self-evolution. These results support an empirical exploration of agentic planning and the aggregate effect of execution-driven harness revisions. Our contributions are: An agentic planning framework that organizes a high-level VLM within an editable harness for sustained task-context management over long horizons, tracking task progress and execution feedback to guide a fixed VLA executor. An execution-driven self-evolution procedure that autonomously proposes and evaluates revisions to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and control rules from rollout feedback, without constructing an SFT dataset. We evaluate SERA on RoboMME and achieve 51.38 overall success. Harness self-evolution improves success by 7.00 percentage points over the initial configuration. Related Work sec:related-work Memory-Augmented Policies Generalist robot policies learn language-conditioned manipulation from diverse data~ brohan2022rt1,openx2023rtx,octo2024octo . VLA models connect pretrained vision-language representations with action learning ( ; ). Related embodied models, including PaLM-E, incorporate visual and continuous state inputs into language models for embodied reasoning and planning driess2023palme . These developments provide a foundation for language-conditioned manipulation, while history-dependent tasks additionally require information beyond the current observation. Recent work has also emphasized the importance of historical information in manipulation, with benchmarks such as RoboMME explicitly evaluating history-dependent behavior~ dai2026robomme . Memory-augmented policies incorporate such information through different representations and update mechanisms~ fang2025sam2act . HAMLET aggregates compact moment tokens across timesteps to condition action prediction~ koo2025hamlet . MemoryVLA retrieves perceptual and cognitive information from a memory bank and fuses it with current representations~ shi2025memoryvla , while ContextVLA compresses past observations into a context token for efficient multi-frame conditioning~ jang2025contextvla . Other designs address cross-subtask information transfer through event-triggered latent memory in WeaveLA~ zhu2026weavela , hierarchical experience retrieval in ECHO~ hu2026echo , and temporal aggregation through frame- and chunk-level recurrent queries in ReMem-VLA~ li2026rememvla . These methods integrate historical information into action prediction through compact temporal representations, memory retrieval, or recurrent updates. Hierarchical Robotic Planning Hierarchical approaches connect high-level reasoning to executable robot behavior through intermediate decisions~ rana2023sayplan,shi2025hirobot,zhang2026lingbotva2 . SayCan combines language-model planning with affordance estimates for pretrained skills ahn2022saycan , and Inner Monologue incorporates environment feedback into subsequent planning~ huang2022innermonologue . Code as Policies expresses robot behavior as programs invoking perception and control APIs liang2023codeaspolicies . Other interfaces include the spatial value maps of VoxPoser, the relational keypoint constraints of ReKep, and the language motions of RT-H huang2023voxposer,huang2024rekep,belkhale2024rth . RoboPARA further uses dependency graphs and resource constraints to organize parallel dual-arm execution~ duan2025robopara . Memory and hierarchical planning can also be combined. MemER trains a high-level VLM to nominate historical keyframes and predict language subtasks; selected keyframes inform subsequent decisions, while a low-level VLA executes the subtasks~ sridhar2025memer . Goal2Skill combines structured task memory with subtask verification and replanning in a VLM--VLA hierarchy liu2026goal2skill . Agentic Embodied Systems and Self-Evolution Research on language models and agents studies reasoning, interaction, and feedback-driven refinement~ madaan2023selfrefine . ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions and observations~ yao2023react ; Reflexion stores textual feedback for subsequent attempts~ shinn2023reflexion ; and Voyager accumulates reusable executable skills through interaction in Minecraft wang2024voyager . Related methods improve prompts or agent code using execution feedback~ agrawal2025gepa,zhang2025dgm . These works provide precedents for agent loops and experience reuse, although their evaluation settings differ from robotic manipulation. Recent embodied systems place these ideas around learned executors~ ahn2024autort . Harness VLA combines a frozen VLA primitive with analytic primitives and task-specific and global memories~ zhang2026harnessvla . HarnessWAM maintains evidence-grounded task state and a task graph, and compiles plans into capability-constrained WAM skills gu2026harnesswam . RoboMemory combines spatial, temporal, episodic, and semantic memories with a planner--critic loop~ lei2025robomemory . HELM couples episodic memory with a learned state verifier and recovery control around a frozen VLA~ zeng2026helm . Cortex combines task-context memory and skill constraints in a deployment harness~ peng2026cortex . Execution-driven harness adaptation is also an emerging research direction. ETA studies experience-derived strategy and skill updates subject to runtime checks before promotion~ chen2026eta . SHAPER evolves textual skills and a context-code harness using rollout feedback and validation while keeping its planner and executor frozen wang2026shaper . Zetta revises runtime critics, recovery playbooks, and executable tools from failed rollouts~ ding2026zetta . Within this line of work, SERA explores an editable harness for high-level planning in history-dependent robotic manipulation. The harness supports within-episode context management and is revised using development-stage execution experience, with the selected version fixed before testing. title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience
summary: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro The same visual scene can pose very different reasoning problems. A visible attribute may be read directly, an object-relative direction requires a reference frame, and a distance estimate may require geometric evidence from several views. Route questions additionally require keeping track of successive movements. Spatial benchmarks expose these differences through multi-image reasoning, limited-view scene construction, dynamic spatial aptitude, and degraded observations~ Yang2025mmsi,Wang2025mindcube,Jia2025omnispatial,Ray2024dynamic,Zhou2026spacedg . A useful reasoner must therefore choose the computation as well as produce the answer. Reconstructing every scene can add unnecessary cost and noisy evidence, while answering directly can overlook information that must be integrated across views. Spatial representations learned through training~ Chen2024spatialvlm,Cheng2024spatialrgpt and tools for perception, reconstruction, and simulation~ Marsili2025visual,Chen2025geometrically,Cho2026spatialclaw,Zhu2026thinking expand the computations available to a reasoner. Agent methods also retain reflections and reusable workflows from earlier tasks~ Shinn2023reflexion,Wang2023voyager,Zhao2023expel,Wang2024agent . Access to a resource, however, does not specify when it is useful. A procedure for computing relative directions can be reused across scenes; the coordinates on which it previously operated cannot. The challenge is to retain experience that informs resource use while grounding each answer in the current scene. SpatialBrain separates scene evidence, reusable computation, and experience about resource use. It operates as an agent: a vision-language reasoner that can select and call tools. After completing tasks, it retains abstract records of the conditions encountered, resources used, and execution feedback. Later tasks consult these records to choose a reasoning route, memory-access mode, or skill. We call this cross-task adaptation self-evolution. The model weights remain fixed; the external experience available to the controller changes. Unlike correcting an answer within one task, self-evolution changes the state available to subsequent tasks. Our core contributions address three parts of this reasoning process (Figure~ fig:spatialbrain-experience-loop ): 3DFusionMemory grounds reasoning in a shared scene state by fusing object, pose, camera, and route observations into queryable spatial evidence with supporting views and uncertainty. Spatial Skill Library makes recurring spatial computations reusable through parameterized tool procedures, separating the operation from the scene-specific inputs on which it acts. Spatial Cognition accumulates condition-specific experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Past process feedback and costs inform resource selection, connecting completed trajectories to later reasoning decisions. Tasks within a block share prior experience and maintain separate scene memories. Updates occur after the block finishes, without reference answers. Evaluation with GPT-5.6-sol shows improvements over direct answers on four of five benchmarks and a tie on the fifth. Component comparisons and execution traces examine resource use and how earlier experience changes later decisions. Related Work sec:related Spatial intelligence. SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT develop spatial representations through targeted supervision~ Chen2024spatialvlm,Cheng2024spatialrgpt , while Thinking in Space studies cognitive maps for video reasoning~ Yang2024thinking . Tool-based approaches expose visual programs, geometric constraints, stateful computation, and simulation to a reasoner~ Hu2024visual,Marsili2025visual,Chen2025geometrically,Cho2026spatialclaw,Zhu2026thinking . Structured representations include S-Agent's scene and agent memories and AlloSpatial's allocentric maps~ Dai2026sagent,Ruan2026allospatial . SpatialCLI provides specialist tools, and SATURN and OmniView-Space emphasize perspective-aware reasoning~ Zhou2026spatialcli,Kamali2026saturn,Li2026omniviewspace . SpatialBrain uses execution experience to decide when and how to invoke spatial representations and computations. Agent skills and memory. Executable skills and recurring workflows provide reusable computation, as in Voyager and Agent Workflow Memory~ Wang2023voyager,Wang2024agent . Skill-3D distills scene-aware tool workflows and failure lessons from rollouts for skill-guided inference and agentic post-training~ Li2026skill3d . SpatialBrain focuses on blockwise, reference-label-free test-time resource adaptation with fixed model weights, separating current-scene geometry from persistent resource-use experience. Episodic reflection and linked memory notes retain broader experience~ Park2023generative,Xu2025amem , whereas object-centric scene graphs and exploration snapshots retain spatial evidence~ Gu2023conceptgraphs,Yang2024scene . In SpatialBrain, the Skill Library stores how to execute a procedure, strategic experience records when and how to use it, and 3DFusionMemory represents what the current scene supports. Self-evolving agents. Self-evolving agents differ in what they update. Reflexion retains verbal feedback for subsequent trials~ Shinn2023reflexion , while ExpeL distills experience from training tasks for later inference~ Zhao2023expel . Agentic Context Engineering consolidates contextual playbooks through generation, reflection, and curation~ Zhang2025ace . Automated Design of Agentic Systems searches agent programs using an expanding archive~ Hu2024adas , while the Darwin G\"odel Machine modifies and tests agent code~ Zhang2025dgm . SpatialBrain updates external spatial strategies and procedural records from completed test-time trajectories. Spatial Cognition selects the reasoning route and access to memory and skills. Tool observations populate the scene memory, and skills carry out reusable computations on the current inputs. An execution trajectory records these decisions, calls, returned evidence, and process checks. Completed trajectories supply experience for later tasks without updating model weights, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:architecture . This separation gives two timescales of state: scene evidence changes within a task, while experience about using evidence changes between task blocks. The memory for the current task is where contains object nodes, spatial relations, camera states, and ordered route history. Repeated observations support the same node, while complementary views add objects that a single view does not cover. Relations are then computed between these fused object representations (Figure~ fig:multiview-memory ). Queries return distances and camera- or object-frame relations together with confidence, supporting views, and ambiguity. Ordered route state supports successive translations and rotations. Spatial Skill Library subsec:skill-library Recurring spatial operations can reuse a computation even when the objects and images change. The library represents each skill as a procedure with an explicit applicability condition and input--output interface: In , specifies applicability, typed input requirements, a parameterized tool procedure, and its returned evidence. For example, a relative-direction procedure binds a reference frame before computing a displacement. Its parameters refer to the current task's objects, so the same procedure can operate on different scenes. Seed skills initialize the library. Completed trajectories add recurring execution patterns and records of their use. Spatial Cognition can withhold a skill, expose it as a planning hint, or permit execution. A change in an existing skill's availability is consequently distinct from the creation of new skill code. title: DisasterRoute: Evidence-Guided Dual-System Routing for Visual Disaster Question Answering
summary: Visual question answering from low-altitude UAV imagery must deliver timely and accurate judgments to support disaster response under limited edge computing resources. Routine questions may be answered through direct decisions, whereas more challenging questions may benefit from step-by-step reasoning. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving models' visual understanding and generative reasoning capabilities, with limited exploration of efficient direct decision-making and its adaptive coordination with generative reasoning. We develop Disaster-S1 based on a vision-language model adapted to the disaster domain. Trained for option discrimination, it outputs a probability distribution over answer options in a single multimodal forward pass for fast decision-making. We further propose DisasterRoute, a dual-system routing framework that combines prediction confidence with disaster evidence to decide whether to accept the initial answer or invoke the disaster reasoning model DisasterVL for review. By allocating inference computation on demand, the framework retains the efficiency of direct decision-making and improves overall question-answering accuracy through selective review. Experiments on DisasterBench show that Disaster-S1 achieves superior accuracy with low latency, while DisasterRoute further improves accuracy through selective review at substantially lower latency than full reasoning.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision--language--action (VLA) models connect visual and language understanding to robot control, enabling a single policy to perform diverse manipulation tasks~ zitkovich2023rt2,black2025pi05,bjorck2025groot . Quantitative pouring adds a requirement beyond executing the manipulation sequence: the transferred mass must match a requested amount. This matters in food preparation~ piacenza2022pouring and household drink-serving tasks~ zhu2023pour (Fig.~ fig:setup_overview ). Without online electronic-scale feedback, the robot must infer how much liquid has been transferred and when to return the container upright. During steady pouring, images and robot pose can remain nearly unchanged while mass accumulates, so visually similar states may require either continued pouring or return. We call this ambiguity physical-completion aliasing. Understanding ``pour 200~g'' specifies the goal but does not reveal physical progress, and initiating return does not stop liquid transfer immediately. Whole-task VLA policies typically learn completion implicitly alongside motion. Policies use force or tactile feedback to guide action generation~ yu2025forcevla,zhang2025tavla,xue2025rdp , while FM-VLA encodes force histories as memory tokens~ li2026fmvla . Wrist wrench is informative about liquid transfer, but it also varies with arm motion, container pose, grasp geometry, and liquid dynamics~ piacenza2022pouring . Force conditioning therefore does not by itself define the accumulated physical quantity needed for a stopping decision. Precision-pouring controllers make this quantity explicit by closing the loop on fill level~ schenck2017visual,zhu2023pour , source-mass loss~ piacenza2022pouring , or predicted overpour~ hu2025robocap . Their feedback formulations offer a useful starting point, but generally assume prescribed grasps or constrained motions. The remaining challenge is to integrate quantitative completion into a learned whole-task policy that must also grasp, transport, pour, return, and place the container. Our insight is to treat physical completion as a persistent state separate from motor generation. couples a shared action expert with explicit flow and mass estimation. Boundary-aware supervision distinguishes continued pouring from return at action-chunk boundaries. A recurrent force observer provides temporal belief to the action expert and a dedicated completion head, which fuses this belief with visual, joint, and wrist-wrench histories to estimate transferred mass. The physical estimators are target-independent, while the requested mass conditions the POUR prompt and completion threshold. The controller accounts for liquid transferred during return by triggering return when predicted terminal mass reaches the target. Real-robot comparisons with whole-task VLA and load-based baselines, mechanism ablations, and held-out target interpolation evaluate this formulation, alongside additional container--fluid regimes with independently trained models. title: AirPlayground: Benchmarking Aerial Navigation across Diverse Reconstructed Environments
summary: Large-scale aerial resources provide a foundation for learning navigation across diverse environments. However, existing resources remain limited in providing (1) densely sampled flight demonstrations for learning different policy formulations and (2) broad environment coverage for standardized closed-loop evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for training and evaluating aerial navigation policies across diverse environments. We first construct 94 photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) environments spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation settings, with aligned collision geometry. Building on these environments, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline for automated expert flight collection, yielding 94K demonstrations and 46.5M synchronized observation-state-action samples at 50 Hz. We further provide an extensible API that supports training different policy formulations on this shared corpus and evaluating them under unified protocols in the corresponding environments. We benchmark seven baselines spanning four policy paradigms across three navigation settings in seen and unseen environments, and further examine scaling behavior with ACT. Scaling ACT's training corpus from 5 to 70 scenes raises median success rates on seen and unseen environments from 30.6% and 16.8% to 41.2% and 29.4%, respectively. Through this shared training and evaluation framework, AirPlayground supports analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes. Our analyses highlight the roles of prediction errors, execution protocols, and scene interactions in closed-loop performance.

Introduction Learning-based aerial navigation depends on large-scale, diverse experience to generalize across environments~ zheng2024towards, liu2025citywalker . Acquiring experience through online interaction can be costly and difficult to scale. Offline demonstrations support scaling policy learning without environment interaction during training~ o2024open . Yet policies trained on demonstrations learn from expert states, whereas deployment exposes them to states shaped by their actions~ seo2024mitigating . Small errors can compound through feedback, so accurate imitation does not guarantee reliable navigation. Assessing reliability therefore requires systematic closed-loop evaluation across diverse environments, where policies must respond to the consequences of their actions. To meet these learning and evaluation needs, aerial navigation research has produced both flight datasets and interactive environments. Large-scale datasets such as CityNav and OpenFly provide aerial trajectories for navigation and vision-language learning~ lee2025citynav,gao2026openfly , substantially increasing the scale and diversity of reusable flight experience. In parallel, 3DGS-based embodied platforms make reconstructed real-world scenes available as photorealistic, geometrically grounded environments for interactive navigation~ liu2026wanderland,miao2026towards,xia2026habitat . Recent benchmarks further combine reconstructed environments, collision-aware interaction, and flight trajectories for policy learning and evaluation~ guo2026huge . Despite this progress, two limitations remain in the resources for aerial policy learning and evaluation. (i) Limited dense flight experience. Densely sampled observation--action demonstrations remain limited across diverse real-world environments. Dense supervision captures continuous flight control for learning different action representations, while coverage across scenes exposes policies to varied visual conditions and spatial structures. (ii) Limited standardized evaluation across diverse environments. Standardized closed-loop evaluation remains limited in its coverage of environments with diverse appearances and spatial structures. Indoor spaces, urban outdoor areas, and vegetation present different visibility and obstacle configurations, making evaluation across these settings important for assessing how consistently policies perform beyond a narrow set of scenes. To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for aerial navigation that pairs dense flight experience with photorealistic 3DGS reconstructions and executable geometry. AirPlayground comprises 94 reconstructed scenes spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation environments, with nearly 100K flight demonstrations and 46.5M RGB frames under 50 Hz observation--action supervision. To scale collection, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline, reusable across reconstructed scenes, that models navigable space, samples navigation tasks, and generates expert demonstrations. We further introduce an extensible cross-policy API that adapts the shared corpus to each policy's native representation and maps its outputs to a common control interface under unified evaluation protocols. By linking recorded trajectories to executable scene geometry, AirPlayground also enables analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes. Specifically, AirPlayground makes three main contributions. (i) Dense flight experience paired with executable reconstructions of real-world environments. We pair dense flight demonstrations with photorealistic reconstructions and aligned navigation and collision geometry for policy learning and matched closed-loop execution. (ii) A unified benchmark across navigation policy paradigms. Our extensible API supports shared-data policy training and unified closed-loop evaluation across three navigation settings, while preserving each policy’s native representations and inference structure through adapters. (iii) Cross-policy evaluation and deployment diagnosis. We benchmark seven baselines and analyze offline predictions and closed-loop behavior. These studies show that offline accuracy alone does not fully explain deployment performance and examine how execution horizons and scene geometry affect navigation, demonstrating the benchmark's value beyond performance comparisons. Related Work Aerial Navigation Datasets. Prior work has expanded navigation-level supervision from constrained simulated settings toward larger urban environments, richer tasks, and broader scene coverage~ liu2023aerialvln,wang2025towards,lee2025citynav,liu2026indooruav . More recent efforts scale collection through automated planning and expert trajectory generation~ low2025sous,gao2026openfly,adang2025singer . Other efforts collect fine-grained flight demonstrations for reactive control and long-horizon navigation~ wang2026uav,zheng2026think . Despite these advances, temporally dense flight demonstrations remain limited in scale and environmental coverage, constraining the continuous control experience for training diverse navigation policies. Reconstructed Environments and Navigation Benchmarks. Recent embodied-navigation research uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct photorealistic real-world environments, providing a real-to-sim bridge for policy learning and evaluation~ chhablani2025embodiedsplat,liu2026navgsim,low2025sous,quach2024gaussian . To support collision-aware navigation, these representations are augmented with metric geometry, collision models, and navigation structures, enabling interactive navigation across reconstructed environments~ miao2026towards,he2026seeing,liu2026wanderland,xia2026habitat . Aerial benchmarks also pair 3DGS environments with geometry for collision checking and evaluation: OpenFly spans 18 scenes from multiple rendering sources, while HUGE provides four reconstructed outdoor environments~ gao2026openfly,guo2026huge . These platforms establish important foundations, but broader coverage of reconstructed indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation environments is still needed for systematic cross-scene policy evaluation. Navigation Policy Evaluation. Offline evaluation measures prediction errors against expert demonstrations, while interactive aerial benchmarks assess task success and path efficiency through closed-loop rollouts~ xue2026see,lou2026voln . Studies in autonomous driving and robot manipulation examine this mismatch, including the predictive value of evaluation metrics and task-critical errors~ wang2026open,huang2026critical . This mismatch also depends on how predictions are executed: work on action-chunking policies investigates execution horizons~ zhao2026dynamic , while studies of aerial agents examine how execution mechanisms affect flight outcomes~ xu2026lightweight . However, a systematic understanding of the offline-to-closed-loop gap in aerial navigation remains limited. By pairing flight demonstrations with executable worlds, AirPlayground supports trajectory replay and policy evaluation in corresponding scenes, providing an experimental basis for tracing offline predictions to their closed-loop consequences. An operator walks each site at a steady pace carrying an XGRIDS Lixel P1 PortalCam, a handheld scanner that pairs a wide-field LiDAR with four synchronized cameras, two fisheye and two forward-facing. title: From Association to Decision Value: Testing Paired Instruction Dependence for VLA Corpus Selection
summary: Choosing among robot demonstration corpora is a ranking problem: an upstream diagnostic must preserve which candidates produce better downstream policies, not merely correlate with average performance. We study paired instruction dependence, the rate at which a demonstrator changes its first decision when only the goal changes. Across 136 independently seeded quadruped-navigation corpora, predictions developed on 56 corpora are evaluated prospectively on 80 held-out corpora. The audit is reliable and associated with downstream paired correctness, and lowers mean absolute prediction error when added to a correctness-aware baseline, but the primary proper-log-score increment is +0.059 nats (95% corpus-bootstrap CI [-0.027, 0.133]) and the prespecified top-20% comparison does not establish an incremental selection gain. An exploratory response decomposition suggests a structural source of this predictive-ranking mismatch: under the tested predictor specification, separating both-correct and both-wrong responses yields larger held-out gains than their unsigned switch statistic. Seed-to-seed agreement indicates that the held-out endpoint retains recoverable rank signal. These results show that counterfactual response structure can be reliable and predictive while providing limited incremental decision value in this setting when compressed into an unsigned statistic, motivating diagnostics that preserve outcome-relevant structure and are validated against the decisions they are intended to support.

Introduction sec:introduction The downstream value of a robot demonstration corpus is usually known only after a vision--language--action (VLA) policy has been fine-tuned on it. Evaluating every candidate therefore pays much of the cost that an upstream diagnostic is meant to avoid. The practical question is consequently decision-focused: can a measurement rank candidate corpora well enough to select the ones that will produce better policies? Language-conditioned behavior creates a tempting diagnostic. If two goals require opposite turns from the same observation, a demonstrator that follows language should usually change its decision when the goal changes. We call the resulting switch rate paired instruction dependence, . Unlike ordinary correctness, it uses a controlled same-state intervention and tests whether the response depends on the instruction. This distinction is relevant to generalist VLAs, whose success can otherwise conceal shortcut policies that weakly use language~ geirhos2020shortcut,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,octo2024,black2024pi0 . Dependence, however, is unsigned. A demonstrator can switch in the correct direction for both goals or in the wrong direction. With binary left/right responses, is exactly the sum of these both-correct and both-wrong cases; the observed action makes that identity approximate rather than exact in our data. The relevant question is therefore narrower than whether language sensitivity matters in general: does unsigned same-state response structure improve prediction and selection after marginal demonstrator correctness is known? This question also separates four criteria that are often conflated: A signal may track broad outcome differences or lower mean error while failing to preserve the ordering near a selection cutoff. Figure~ fig:motivation illustrates this decision-value gap. We test it prospectively on 136 independently seeded quadruped-navigation corpora. Nested probabilistic predictors are developed on 56 corpora, while 80 disjoint corpora form the held-out test population. We train 544 adapters across Qwen2.5-VL-3B and Qwen3.5-VL-0.8B and evaluate in-distribution and under a controlled scene shift. The primary selection endpoint is paired first-decision correctness; closed-loop evaluation separately tests how this local endpoint relates to full navigation. Predictors, held-out corpus identifiers, and the top-20 operating point were prespecified before held-out outcomes were revealed. Decision resolution and practical alternatives: a cross-seed resolution benchmark establishes recoverable corpus ordering, while demonstrator and proxy baselines locate the audit relative to realistic selectors. Physical VLM-to-VLA transfer is increasingly practical~ hancock2026actions ; NaVILA separates language-level navigation decisions from low-level legged control~ jiang2024navila , as we do. We study the preceding data decision: which fixed demonstration corpus should train a policy? Language grounding and counterfactual evaluation: Vision-and-language navigation established grounded instruction following~ anderson2018vision , but success can hide instruction-insensitive shortcuts. Controlled tests expose memorized action sequences and semantic failures~ fei2025liberoplus,zhou2026liberopro,hou2026langgap,yu2026robosemanticbench , while mismatched instructions can supply corrective supervision~ kondoh2026counteralign . Our intervention similarly holds the state fixed while changing the goal, but it measures a data-generating demonstrator and predicts a separately trained learner. Crucially, we distinguish unsigned response change from correctness-resolved response structure. Robot-data selection and valuation: Robot policies are sensitive to demonstration composition and scale~ mandlekar2022what,saxena2025whatmatters,lin2025scaling . Data valuation uses marginal contribution, training dynamics, gradients, or standardized retraining~ ghorbani2019datashapley,swayamdipta2020dataset,xia2024less,gadre2023datacomp . title: CausGround: Causal Interaction Grounding for Adaptive Embodied Planning
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promising reasoning capabilities, but reliable physical interaction requires planning that accounts for when actions are executable and how they change the world. These preconditions and effects are environment-dependent and often not captured by MLLMs, making adaptation challenging. Yet existing approaches either require costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to reuse. Therefore, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework that distills interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge. CausGround identifies action preconditions and effects and organizes them in a factorized world-state representation capturing object attributes and inter-object relations. At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in current observations to support backward reasoning over preconditions and forward reasoning over effects for action selection and multi-step planning. We evaluate CausGround on simulated high-level planning, interaction reasoning, and real-world robot manipulation. On adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks, CausGround improves vision-based high-level planning across MLLM backbones, increasing average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and closed-loop planning success from 43.0% to 57.0% on RoboCasa. On SWITCH, average interaction reasoning accuracy increases from 25.8% to 31.9%, indicating improved action selection, recovery, and verification. Moreover, real-world experiments show that CausGround reasons backward from MLLM-interpreted goals to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation. These results demonstrate that reusable action preconditions and effects support long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.

These preconditions and effects are often environment-dependent and are not fully captured by MLLMs, making adaptation to new environments challenging. Yet existing adaptation approaches either update model parameters through costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to ground and reuse. At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in the current observation, supporting backward reasoning over action preconditions and forward reasoning over action effects for action selection and multi-step causal planning. Project Page: Introduction sec:intro Embodied agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising reasoning capabilities for high-level planning~ chen2025planning, driess2023palm, feng2025reflective . Yet successful embodied interaction requires more than knowing what to do: agents must know when an action is executable and how it changes the world. Such interaction knowledge is often environment-dependent, involving available actions, object states, action preconditions, and effects~ kim2025multi, han2024interpret, liu2024learning . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser , a planner may correctly infer that an object should be placed into a fridge, yet attempt the action before satisfying the precondition that the fridge be open. Such precondition violations can accumulate over long-horizon execution, leading to invalid actions, repeated attempts, and costly trial-and-error~ raman2024cape, zhi2025closed, chang2025partnr . Effective embodied planning therefore requires agents to account for task semantics while adapting their planning to the interaction dynamics of the environment in which the task is executed. Existing approaches still fall short in enabling efficient environment adaptation. A direct strategy is to specialize embodied agents through fine-tuning or reinforcement learning~ xu2026roboagent, zhai2024fine, feng2025towards , but such parametric adaptation requires substantial environment-specific interaction data and repeated optimization, making it costly to deploy across diverse environments, particularly in real-world settings. Non-parametric approaches instead incorporate interaction feedback or episodic memory at inference time~ anwar2025remembr , but such experience is often retained as unstructured trajectories or task-level memories~ ginting2025enter, buoso2025select2plan . This makes it difficult to identify which parts of an experience are causally relevant rather than incidental, reuse them across tasks, or ground them in the current visual scene. Moreover, existing representations do not always jointly capture the fine-grained object attributes and inter-object relations required to determine whether an action's preconditions are satisfied~ chen2025planning, shen2026reward . This raises a central question: Can interaction experience be distilled into reusable causal knowledge that tells an embodied agent both what must be true before an action and what changes as a result? To this end, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework for adaptive embodied planning. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser , CausGround abstracts interaction experience into action-centered causal knowledge, representing each action through its relevant preconditions and resulting state effects. Rather than storing complete trajectories, it organizes reusable action-centered causal knowledge over a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations. At planning time, the current observation and task are grounded into the same representation to construct a task-relevant local causal graph from reusable causal knowledge. This allows the planner to reason backward over action preconditions to determine what must happen before an action becomes executable, and forward over state effects to anticipate how the world should change after execution. Composing such causal dependencies provides a structured reference for multi-step planning without updating model parameters. We evaluate CausGround across heterogeneous long-horizon embodied settings. In simulation, we adapt VirtualHome~ puig2018virtualhome and RoboCasa~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 for visually grounded high-level planning and observe consistent improvements under both one-shot and closed-loop planning, including an increase in average task success from 24.9 to 53.3 on VirtualHome and from 43.0 to 57.0 under closed-loop planning on RoboCasa. Beyond simulation, we evaluate interaction reasoning on SWITCH~ cheng2025switch , a real-world egocentric long-horizon interaction benchmark, where CausGround improves average accuracy from 25.8 to 31.9 . We further validate the framework on real-robot manipulation, where CausGround reasons backward from interpreted goal states to derive executable high-level action sequences and successfully complete multi-step interactions. Together, these results show that explicit causal interaction knowledge provides a reusable grounding substrate for long-horizon embodied reasoning across diverse environments. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate embodied interaction knowledge around action preconditions and state effects, and introduce a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations, enabling interaction knowledge to be grounded in current visual observations. We introduce CausGround, a non-parametric framework that distills interaction trajectories into reusable action-centered causal knowledge and dynamically grounds task-relevant causal dependencies for planning. This enables reasoning over both what must hold before an action and how the world changes after it without parameter updates. We evaluate CausGround across long-horizon embodied settings spanning VirtualHome and RoboCasa simulations, the real-world egocentric SWITCH benchmark, and real-robot manipulation, demonstrating consistent gains in planning and interaction reasoning across environments and MLLM backbones. Embodied agents deployed in new environments often need to adjust their behavior based on newly acquired interaction experience. Earlier approaches typically absorb environment-specific experience into model parameters through fine-tuning, imitation learning, or reinforcement learning~ kim2026robot, kang2025gflowvlm, tian2026seea . With the growing capabilities of foundation models, recent work has increasingly explored adaptation without continual parameter updates, using execution feedback~ wang2023voyager , past trajectories~ zhao2024expel , or external memory~ sohn2026r4 to provide environment-specific information during deployment. This shifts environment adaptation from updating the model itself toward leveraging external environment knowledge. Therefore, effective adaptation depends not only on how experience is acquired and accumulated, but also on how the underlying world state is represented. World State Representations for Embodied Planning. Existing world-state representations vary substantially in their level of abstraction. Free-form textual representations can flexibly summarize observations and state changes, but often entangle multiple entities and dynamic properties within a shared description~ hao2023reasoning, chen2025planning . Object-centric representations reduce this entanglement by organizing state information around individual entities~ yoneda2024statler, feng2026learning , while more factorized representations further separate each object into explicit attribute-value pairs, enabling finer-grained state tracking~ shen2026reward, rozanov2025stateact . Yet embodied interaction depends not only on the state of individual objects, but also on relations among them~ ju2026momagraph, gu2024conceptgraphs . Therefore, a world-state representation for embodied planning should jointly capture fine-grained object attributes and explicit inter-object relations, providing a shared basis for grounding observations and environment-specific interaction knowledge. Interaction-Grounded High-Level Planning. A structured world state provides a basis for grounding environment-specific knowledge, but effective planning further requires turning such knowledge into actionable guidance. MLLM-based planners can generate actions or action sequences from current observations and task descriptions~ lv2024robomp, feng2025reflective , leveraging strong pretrained priors to guide task completion. Before committing actions to the environment, world-model-based planners further predict action-conditioned state changes~ li2026word, song2026model and evaluate candidate trajectories through simulation or adaptive latent-space rollouts~ liu2026simpact, yao2026dronewam, RISE , providing lookahead for multi-step decisions. Moreover, dependencies across multiple actions are typically instantiated only through rollout, requiring repeated simulation during planning. title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision--language--action (VLA) models bring pre-trained visual and linguistic representations to robot control~ brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla . After deployment, such a policy keeps encountering tasks, scenes and instructions that its training demonstrations cover only partially. In tasks where failures may be costly, when facing difficulties due to insufficient training knowledge, the robot should respond adaptively by deferring tasks to seek human assistance or by requesting relevant additional training demonstrations~ ross2011dagger,kelly2019hgdagger,hoque2021thriftydagger,hoque2022fleetdagger,liu2023sirius,bagatella2025active,romer2026uqvla . Both responses are effective only if guided by the policy's epistemic uncertainty, that is, by how poorly its training data support a situation. Unlike aleatoric ambiguity, epistemic uncertainty shrinks with more relevant demonstrations~ kendall2017uncertainties,hullermeier2021aleatoric . Flow-based VLAs do not provide such an estimate by themselves. This motivates dedicated methods for quantifying epistemic uncertainty in these policies. For example, romer2026uqvla derive velocity-field disagreement (VFD), an ensemble estimate of the divergence between flow-matching policies. They use VFD in SAVE, an active fine-tuning procedure that they evaluate on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , a simulation benchmark of language-instructed household manipulation tasks. In each round, SAVE requests a few new demonstrations, preferring situations that VFD rates as uncertain, and then fine-tunes the policy. In their evaluation, VFD correlates more strongly with task success than six alternative uncertainty scores, including other ensemble-based measures and entropy-based scores. SAVE with VFD needs at least 22 fewer demonstrations than the compared acquisition strategies. The price is an ensemble of at least two policies: every additional member must be pre-trained, fine-tuned alongside the deployed policy in every adaptation round, and integrated jointly with it whenever a score is computed. We ask whether this ensemble is necessary to obtain comparably useful estimates of epistemic uncertainty. Ensemble disagreement reflects differences between the predictions of independently trained policies, which can arise where the demonstrations leave their behaviour weakly constrained. Their disagreement can therefore serve as an indirect signal of demonstration coverage. This motivates assessing coverage directly in the embedding space of a single trained policy, using lightweight uncertainty estimation heads. Each head reads embeddings that the policy already computes and compares a queried observation with support observations from its training demonstrations (Figure~ fig:architecture ). The approach assumes that the embeddings keep unfamiliar observations apart from familiar ones~ vanamersfoort2021due , a property that we do not enforce during training. Its practical usefulness further depends on whether unfamiliarity helps identify situations where the policy may fail or benefit from assistance or additional demonstrations. We assess these relationships empirically across our experiments. The measure is the posterior variance of a Gaussian process (GP) with a Gaussian kernel, conditioned on the support embeddings~ rasmussen2006gpml . It needs no regression targets and no gradient update and does not alter the policy's predicted actions but can inform decisions such as when to request help or new demonstrations. Fitting it post hoc to a trained policy takes one feature extraction pass over the support observations and one Cholesky factorization. Since the heads are this cheap, several of them can be attached to different embeddings of the same policy. Heads on modality-specific representations, such as the camera or instruction tokens, can then indicate which part of an input is unfamiliar. We organize the study around five questions. Does a single-policy kernel variance head match ensemble scores in calibration to task success and referral gain to a stronger supervisor on LIBERO-10? Here, referral means handing the most uncertain situations to a more capable supervisor policy, which serves as a proxy for human assistance. Does active fine-tuning with the SAVE protocol guided by kernel variance scores acquire demonstrations as effectively as ensemble scores? How much computation does the kernel variance head save compared to ensemble scores? Which properties of an uncertainty score do the established evaluations of Q1 reward on LIBERO? Do kernel variance heads on different context embeddings respond selectively to perturbations of the inputs they read, and do kernel variance heads support within-task referral under such perturbations? In addressing these questions, we make three contributions: Post-hoc epistemic uncertainty heads that read the embeddings of a single trained VLA policy. Instead of pre-training, fine-tuning and running a second policy, they require only one feature extraction pass over the support observations and one matrix factorization. In our experiments, this makes the heads up to about 44 times faster to set up per fine-tuning round and up to about 50 times faster to use. A comparison on the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, in which the kernel variance heads perform comparably to uncertainty scores from a two-policy ensemble in ranking tasks by their failure rate and in selecting new training demonstrations, following the setting of prior ensemble-based work~ romer2026uqvla . We additionally evaluate success gain from handing uncertain situations over to a stronger policy, where the kernel variance heads again match or exceed the ensemble. Our analysis shows that in this setting, the evaluations mainly test whether a score recognizes how well training demonstrations cover a task, which is useful in itself. However, they test the ranking of situations within a task only weakly, because relatively large execution noise obscures reproducible differences in the outcomes. A within-task evaluation that perturbs single input modalities and their combinations in a controlled way. In this evaluation, our uncertainty heads detect most perturbations at least as sensitively as the ensemble scores and match or exceed them in deciding which situations within a task to hand over to a stronger policy. Attached to the embeddings of separate input modalities, context-specific uncertainty heads also indicate which of them are unfamiliar. Section~ sec:related places the heads among distance-aware uncertainty estimators, uncertainty scores for generative policies, and work on active data acquisition and deferral. Section~ sec:methods defines the kernel-variance heads on SmolVLA and their context-specific variants, the SAVE acquisition loop, the calibration and referral metrics, our matched experimental protocol and the controlled perturbations of single input modalities. Section~ sec:results first compares the heads with the ensemble scores in task-level calibration, demonstration acquisition and its cost, and supervisor referral (Q1--Q3). It then examines which properties of a score the established evaluations reward (Q4) and evaluates the context-specific and whole-policy heads under controlled perturbations (Q5). Section~ sec:discussion discusses the five research questions in turn, then further findings, such as why unfamiliarity does not imply failure, and the limitations of our study. VLAs often fine-tune vision-language backbones on large robot datasets~ oneill2024oxe and output actions as discrete tokens~ brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla or through continuous generative heads~ octo2024,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla . Flow-matching action experts~ lipman2023flow , like diffusion policies~ chi2023diffusion , sample action chunks from multimodal distributions. On LIBERO~ liu2023libero , a widely used simulation benchmark for these models, high scores may reflect memorized layouts and instructions and do not necessarily imply robustness under changed object positions, cameras, lighting or wording~ zhou2025liberopro,fei2025liberoplus . This motivates evaluations that vary conditions within a task (Sections~ sec:results-benchmark -- sec:results-perturbed ). Epistemic uncertainty and distance awareness. Epistemic uncertainty reflects limited knowledge about the true function, whereas aleatoric uncertainty reflects inherent randomness in the data and cannot be reduced by collecting more~ kendall2017uncertainties,hullermeier2021aleatoric . For expressive models, epistemic uncertainty is mainly uncertainty about which of the many functions that fit the data is correct, so it is large where data sparsity leaves predictions weakly constrained ~ hullermeier2021aleatoric . For a robot policy, it concerns which actions the training demonstrations imply in a given situation, while aleatoric uncertainty arises, for example, when demonstrators solve a task in several valid ways or when contact outcomes are stochastic. A principled estimate may approximate the posterior over functions and measures the spread of its predictions~ blattmann2025implicit . Weight-space methods such as deep ensembles~ lakshminarayanan2017ensembles , Monte Carlo dropout~ gal2016dropout and Laplace approximations~ kristiadi2020bayesian,daxberger2021laplace define the prior over functions only implicitly through the weights. title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Added project website to abstract and updated author affiliation; research content unchanged
summary: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced. Project website: https://rangenav.github.io/.

title: AOV-GS: Active Open-Vocabulary Semantic Mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables. Published at AIST 2026
summary: Robots deployed in human-centered environments need maps that support both geometric navigation and open-vocabulary semantic queries beyond a fixed label set. A key challenge is enriching such maps with semantic information without relying on manually annotated segmentation masks or closed-set semantic categories. Existing geometry-driven active mapping maximizes coverage but treats semantics as a passive by-product of the collected trajectory, whereas active semantic mapping typically depends on supervised semantic segmentation. We present AOV-GS, an active 3D Gaussian mapping system that guides exploration using frozen foundation models. During coarse exploration, AOV-GS re-ranks geometrically promising candidate views according to CLIP mask-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance segmentation, biasing exploration toward semantically informative regions. Frozen SAM and CLIP provide instance masks and language-aligned embeddings throughout mapping, while a lightweight scene-specific language field is fitted offline directly to the collected CLIP embeddings rather than manually annotated masks, enabling open-vocabulary text-query segmentation on novel views. In a controlled comparison using the same SAM-CLIP perception stack, AOV-GS improves average language-field mIoU over geometry-only active planning by 1.3 percentage points on Replica (34.6% on eight scenes) and by 1.8 points on Matterport3D (23.1% on five scenes). With CorrCLIP, AOV-GS reaches 35.6% on Replica, 2.0 points above the matched Geometry-based + CorrCLIP baseline. Novel-view PSNR remains comparable to the geometry-only baseline on both datasets while depth L1 improves on Replica. Code is available at https://github.com/OptimusFaber/AOV-GS.

Introduction Mobile robots operating in human-centered environments need spatial maps of the environment that support both navigation and task-level semantic interaction. In practice this means a map should render high-quality RGB-D views and support queries such as find the chair or locate the table near the window. These objectives are coupled through exploration: the viewpoints collected during mapping determine geometric completeness, object visibility, and the evidence available for downstream open-vocabulary retrieval. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM systems~ kerbl20233dgaussiansplatting,keetha2024splatam achieve efficient high-fidelity reconstruction suitable for online robotic mapping. Active planners such as ActiveGS~ jin2025activegs , ActiveSplat~ li2025activesplat , and ActiveGAMER~ chen2025activegamer improve coverage through geometry-aware next-best-view (NBV) selection. In parallel, foundation-model perception enables open-vocabulary semantics: Segment Anything (SAM)~ kirillov2023segment provides prompt-free instance masks and CLIP~ radford2021learning maps mask regions to a language-aligned embedding space. LangSplat~ qin2024langsplat and related methods attach such features to 3D primitives for text-query segmentation, but typically assume a fixed observation trajectory. Active semantic mapping closes part of this gap. ActiveSGM~ chen2025activesgm demonstrates that semantic signals can guide exploration in a 3DGS loop, but relies on per-scene OneFormer~ jain2023oneformer fine-tuning, which limits open-vocabulary deployment. Passive fusion pipelines~ jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion,peng2023openscene can improve semantic quality on pre-recorded trajectories but do not affect online data acquisition. This paper addresses the following question: Can a robot actively explore an unseen scene using frozen foundation models, improve open-vocabulary segmentation through viewpoint selection, and preserve competitive RGB-D reconstruction quality? We answer affirmatively with AOV-GS (Fig.~ fig:pipeline_neuro ). During coarse exploration (stage~0), geometric information gain is augmented with CLIP-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance masks on RGB views rendered from the current Gaussian map. Semantic novelty is measured against a growing keyframe embedding bank and re-ranks the top- geometrically strong candidates. During refinement (stage~1+), planning reverts to geometry-only behavior as in ActiveGS~ jin2025activegs . After exploration, per-keyframe CLIP mask embeddings train a sparse language field on Gaussian primitives, enabling open-vocabulary text-query segmentation on novel views. As in ActiveSGM, candidate RGB views for semantic scoring are rendered from the current Gaussian map; Habitat supplies the posed RGB-D observation after the selected view is executed. The experiments nevertheless use ground-truth camera poses as oracle SLAM input. Our contributions are: A coarse exploration NBV criterion that re-ranks the top- candidates produced by the geometric planner according to CLIP mask-embedding novelty, steering the robot toward semantically novel object instances while reverting to geometry-only scoring during later refinement stages. An active open-vocabulary semantic mapping pipeline combining online semantic exploration with offline LangSplatV2 language-field construction, without per-scene segmenter fine-tuning. A two-benchmark evaluation showing average open-vocabulary gains over geometry-only exploration while preserving comparable novel-view reconstruction quality. title: SP-HLM: Sparse-Pose-Driven Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our \href{https://sp-hlm.github.io/}{\textcolor{blue}{project page}}.

Additional results and videos are available on our project page . INTRODUCTION The motion interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control is an important design choice in humanoid loco-manipulation ~ jiang2025wholebodyvla,yin2025visualmimic, chen2026unit . Existing interfaces emphasize different aspects of humanoid motion. Joint-space actions~ hu2026openhlm,wei2026psi0, xiao2026rove directly specify joint configurations, but can require the high-level policy to model whole-body coordination alongside task intent. Task-space actions provide a compact, task-grounded representation, yet sparse targets alone do not fully specify coordinated whole-body motion. Token-space actions~ luo2026sonic can encode reusable coordination patterns, while task-critical spatial targets may remain implicit. These trade-offs motivate an interface that combines representations of spatial intent and whole-body coordination, rather than encoding both in a single form. We argue that task-critical spatial intent and whole-body coordination should instead be represented in complementary forms. Spatial intent remains explicit, specifying where task-relevant body parts should move, whereas whole-body coordination is encoded implicitly as a learned motion prior describing how the body should move. Following this principle, we expose only five task-critical body poses---the pelvis, two wrists, and two ankles---as explicit spatial constraints and complement them with a latent whole-body motion representation. This interface preserves direct task-space control while avoiding the need for the high-level policy to explicitly specify full-body coordination. Following this formulation, we present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. At its core, SP-GMT performs whole-body control by jointly conditioning on sparse task-space targets and a learned motion latent. We pretrain a motion variational autoencoder (VAE) to encode full-body motion into a compact latent representation. This latent provides coordination information not fully specified by the sparse targets while enabling efficient policy training. To obtain this implicit motion prior from sparse task-space targets at deployment, we introduce SP-MGM, which reconstructs coordinated full-body motion from five-point pose targets in real time. Starting from a pretrained motion generation model, SP-MGM reduces network depth and denoising steps and employs two-stage distillation to improve sparse-pose adherence and temporal consistency. The proposed interface also reduces the burden of high-level action prediction. SP-VLA predicts only task-relevant sparse body poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions, without directly predicting full-body configurations. We further adopt asynchronous action-chunk inference for responsive closed-loop execution. Together, SP-VLA specifies task-space intent, SP-MGM recovers coordinated whole-body motion, and SP-GMT integrates the explicit sparse targets and implicit motion prior for whole-body control. We separately evaluate SP-GMT, SP-MGM, and the complete SP-HLM system. SP-GMT achieves competitive motion-tracking performance against representative state-of-the-art baselines. SP-MGM improves sparse-pose adherence over the motion-generation baseline while achieving a 1.45 higher generation rate. For loco-manipulation, SP-HLM achieves a 52.75 overall success rate across eight simulated tasks, outperforming the token-space and joint-space baselines. We further validate SP-HLM on four real-world tasks, demonstrating its feasibility for humanoid loco-manipulation. Our main contributions are: We propose a sparse-pose-driven motion interface for humanoid loco-manipulation, combining five task-critical body poses with a learned motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. We develop SP-GMT, a whole-body tracker conditioned jointly on sparse targets and a pretrained motion representation, and SP-MGM, a real-time sparse-conditioned motion generator trained through two-stage distillation. We present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework that integrates the above two components with SP-VLA, which uses asynchronous action-chunk inference to predict task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint-position targets from multimodal inputs. The resulting system achieves higher overall success than the evaluated baselines across eight simulated tasks and is further validated on four real-world tasks. RELATED WORK General Humanoid Motion Generation and Control Recent work increasingly uses motion generation as an intermediate layer between high-level semantic commands and low-level humanoid control, typically producing dense whole-body references for downstream tracking~ xie2026textop,jiang2025uniact,huang2026omg . Some methods formulate motion synthesis as an in-betweening problem~ wang2026motionbricks , whereas others employ generative models as online motion planners~ zhang2026wholebody,chen2026reactivebfm . Although these approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of generative motion priors for hierarchical control, they largely rely on dense motion references rather than explicit task-space interfaces tailored to loco-manipulation. In parallel, general motion tracking has emerged as a scalable approach to acquiring versatile whole-body control from large and diverse motion corpora~ luo2026sonic,chen2025gmt,li2026omnitrack,zhang2025track . Recent studies improve generalization by scaling motion data and model capacity~ qi2026generative,qi2026humanoidgpt,chen2026holomotion,zeng2026scaling , while others leverage heterogeneous motion sources or expert specialization~ sleiman2026zest,pan2025agility,wang2026experts . Related efforts learn reusable behavioral representations that can be transferred to downstream control tasks~ li2026bfm,liao2025beyondmimic . Together, these advances provide increasingly general and robust motion generation and control capabilities, while the interface for conveying task-relevant whole-body intent from high-level loco-manipulation policies remains comparatively less explored. Motion Interfaces for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation sec:related_hlm Recent humanoid loco-manipulation systems increasingly pursue unified whole-body behaviors through vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ jiang2025wholebodyvla,wei2026psi0,hu2026openhlm,gu2026haf,liu2025trajbooster , world-action models~ zheng2026motionwam,li2026omega , and perceptive reinforcement policies~ yin2025visualmimic,he2025viral . Beyond the choice of policy architecture, an important design consideration is the motion interface through which task-level intent is conveyed to whole-body execution. Existing approaches span decoupled upper- and lower-body control~ wei2026psi0,jiang2025wholebodyvla and explicit whole-body kinematic representations~ wang2026vlk,hu2026openhlm . While these interfaces provide direct control over robot motion, they can require the high-level policy to reason over relatively detailed body configurations. Other methods adopt more compact learned motion representations, such as motion tokens~ zheng2026motionwam,xue2025leverb , which capture reusable coordination patterns but make task-relevant spatial constraints less explicit. Recent work also explores compact task-space interfaces based on sparse body targets or low-rate task-space trajectories, leaving the remaining whole-body coordination to downstream controllers~ yang2026handoff,ge2026cwi,liu2026learning . title: From Reasoning to Action: Benchmarking Frontier AI Models on LIBERO-10 Robot Manipulation Tasks

summary: Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark. Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end-effector poses and gripper commands, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini-4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%. Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions. These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.
