Introduction Recent advances in frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use~ arena2026leaderboard . In particular, recent demonstrations of GPT-6 Astra have shown impressive robot manipulation behaviors, including interpreting visual observations, generating robot actions, and correcting mistakes through closed-loop interaction~ zhang2026unexpected,su2026astra,team2026systematically . NVIDIA's Astranomy report~ yang2026astranomy further demonstrates the potential of frontier AI models for robot manipulation through different control configurations, including direct action generation, agentic tool use, and supervision of pretrained robot policies. These results suggest that general-purpose AI models may be capable of performing robot manipulation without task-specific policy training. Despite these promising demonstrations, an important question remains: How well do frontier AI models perform on established robot manipulation benchmarks? Existing evaluations often use different tasks, robot platforms, and control interfaces, making systematic comparisons difficult. Connecting frontier AI models to standardized benchmarks is essential for understanding their capabilities, identifying limitations, and comparing their performance with conventional robot learning approaches. Motivated by this question, we develop a unified manipulation pipeline to evaluate frontier AI models on LIBERO-10 (also known as LIBERO-Long)~ liu2023libero , a subset of LIBERO-100 containing ten held-out, long-horizon manipulation tasks. LIBERO-10 has been widely adopted for evaluating robot learning methods, including generalist robot policies and vision-language-action models such as Octo~ team2024octo , OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , ~ intelligence2025pi_ , UniVLA~ bu2025univla and UniAct~ zheng2025universal . Built upon the open-source Inspect Robots framework~ inspect-robots , our pipeline enables frontier AI models to interact with the simulation environment through visual observations and structured tool calls, allowing closed-loop manipulation without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We evaluate multiple frontier AI models, including GPT and Claude models, under a common protocol, exploring different reasoning modes to investigate the impact of reasoning effort on manipulation performance. Beyond task success rates, we analyze API calls, inference latency, token usage, and monetary cost to understand the tradeoffs between reasoning capabilities, manipulation performance, and efficiency. Our work provides a standardized evaluation of frontier AI models on robot manipulation tasks, offering insights into their capabilities and limitations. By releasing our code and evaluation results, we provide reproducible, ready-to-use baselines for future research, reducing the need to repeatedly evaluate these computationally expensive models and lowering evaluation costs. Closed-Loop Manipulation with Frontier AI Models sec:method We evaluate frontier AI models, including GPT-6, Claude Opus, and Gemini, directly as closed-loop robot manipulation policies, without robot-specific training, demonstrations, or pretrained skill libraries. Unlike approaches that use AI models to generate robot code or orchestrate predefined skills~ xiao2026enpire,lu2026aspire,chen2026gap,ora2026 , our pipeline focuses on evaluating the models' intrinsic visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and action planning capabilities. Given raw camera observations, the models must identify objects, estimate their 3D positions, and plan robot motions through a minimal action interface, without relying on external perception, planning, or manipulation skills. This design allows us to assess how effectively frontier AI models can translate their own reasoning into robot actions. Figure~ fig:framework illustrates our closed-loop manipulation pipeline. At each interaction step, the model receives a fixed system prompt, the task instruction, the interaction history, and the latest observation, including camera images and robot state information (Sec.~ sec:observations ). Based on these inputs, the model generates a single tool call: move to specifies a target end-effector pose and gripper command, while done and give up terminate the episode (Sec.~ sec:actions ). For each move to call, an action adapter translates the target into a sequence of low-level robot commands, which are executed step by step in the LIBERO simulator. Task success is checked after every control step. If the task remains incomplete after the action sequence finishes, updated observations and execution feedback are returned to the model for the next decision (Sec.~ sec:evaluation ). This process continues until the task succeeds, the model terminates the episode, or the evaluation limits are reached. All experiments are conducted in a zero-shot setting, using a task-agnostic system prompt without task-specific hints or demonstrations. Observations and Prompt Context sec:observations Observations. Each observation contains two RGB images, from the fixed third-person (agentview) camera and the wrist camera, together with the robot state. The robot state has 12 values: the end-effector position in meters in the world frame, its orientation in the 6D rotation representation (the first two columns of the rotation matrix), the current gripper command, and the two measured finger positions. The gripper command only records whether the model last asked the gripper to open or close; the measured finger positions show where the fingers actually stopped, so the model can tell whether it closed on an object or on nothing. Each observation is sent as one message: the robot state as text, followed by the two labeled camera images. The model never sees object poses or the success signal. System prompt. The system prompt, reproduced verbatim in Figure~ fig:prompt , has two parts. The first part is a generic agent instruction that is independent of the robot and the task: it explains the tool-call interface, requires exactly one tool call per turn with a short note on every motion, tells the model when to call done or give up, and states the budget of 80 LLM calls. The second part, appended under Embodiment notes, contains the environment guidelines that we wrote for LIBERO. They describe the robot, the coordinate frame, the rotation representation, the gripper behavior, and the available sensing, followed by eight general manipulation rules. The same prompt is used for all ten tasks and all models; only the embodiment name changes with the task. The task instruction is not part of the system prompt. It is LIBERO's original natural-language task description, which the model receives as the first user message and again at the top of every observation message. The instructions of all ten tasks are listed in Figure~ fig:taskgallery . Interaction history. Each LLM call is stateless, so every call resends the fixed context (the system prompt and the task instruction), followed by the interaction history accumulated so far. Text and images in this history are treated differently. The text history is complete: it contains the text part of every observation since the start of the episode (the task instruction and the 12 robot-state values), the model's own tool calls and notes, and the execution feedback of each call. Images, in contrast, are kept only for the two most recent observations (the previous and current observations in Figure~ fig:framework ), i.e., at most four images per call; the images of all earlier observations are replaced by a short text placeholder. Because each call adds one observation, the length of the history is bounded by the budget of 80 LLM calls. Action Interface and Execution sec:actions Tools. The tool calls are generated through the native function-calling interface of each model's API: every request includes the name, description, and argument format of each tool, and the model replies with a structured call that names one tool and gives its arguments in JSON, which the framework then executes. title: LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces
summary: Interactive video world models predict how an environment evolves under user actions, but most existing systems assume one controlled agent and one task-specific action interface. We study multi-agent video world modeling, where one model generates a joint visual future for multiple controlled agents while interpreting heterogeneous controls ranging from binary game buttons to continuous robot commands. This task presents two complementary challenges. First, every agent-indexed action stream must control its intended visual entity independently. Second, the model must adapt the meaning of each control variable across different tasks, where the same tensor dimension may denote an attack, steering command, or robot command. We introduce LiveAct, centered on a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI) whose two components mirror this decomposition. To support independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation uses language-driven spatial gates and agent-specific attention to bind each action stream to its intended visual agent. To accommodate heterogeneous controls, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation describes each control variable in language and modulates its semantic token with the synchronized numerical value. We further transfer the complete interface to a blockwise causal generator through teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching, enabling efficient streaming generation while retaining agent-specific control and action semantics. We instantiate the formulation on six multi-agent sources spanning games and multi-robot manipulation, and evaluate visual quality, action following, agent attribution, and latency. Across games and robot manipulation, LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without agent locations or identity crops, and the causal generator attains 17.70 FPS at $512\times 448$.

title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6 and 4.0 over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5 over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3 . These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks. Introduction Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ beyer2024paligemmaversatile3bvlm, deitke2024molmopixmoopenweights, yang2025qwen3technicalreport have established Vision–Language–Action (VLA)~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing, liu2025rdt1bdiffusionfoundationmodel models as a prominent paradigm for robotic manipulation. Although imitation learning (IL) from large-scale robot demonstrations enables VLA models to acquire diverse manipulation skills, its performance is inherently constrained by the coverage of the demonstration data. Reinforcement learning (RL) overcomes this limitation by directly optimizing policies with task feedback obtained through environment interaction, and recent work~ li2026simplevla,xu2026rltokenbootstrappingonline has successfully applied RL to VLA models. However, existing VLA-RL methods still face substantial challenges in long-horizon manipulation tasks. First, most methods rely on terminal-only success rewards. In an episode that completes the first subtasks but fails at subtask , the absence of a terminal success reward causes generalized advantage estimation (GAE) to propagate failure-related temporal-difference (TD) residuals backward to , suppressing the advantages of correctly executed actions. We refer to this as credit contamination, where useful behavior in failed trajectories is systematically devalued, with the effect worsening as the horizon grows. Prior work~ chen2025robohorizonllmassistedmultiviewworld, yang2026actorcriticcontinuousactionchunks, tan2025robodopaminegeneralprocessreward, zhai2025visionlanguageactioncriticmodelroboticrealworld mitigates reward sparsity through stage-level preference optimization or subtask-level intermediate rewards, but these approaches alter reward density without resolving credit contamination. Second, subtask mastery is uneven, with failures increasingly concentrated in a few bottleneck subtasks during later training. Uniform task sampling and fixed exploration then waste interaction budget on saturated subtasks while providing insufficient exploration for the bottlenecks. sec:intro To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, as illustrated in Fig.~ teaser , an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure. Our key insight is that semantic subtasks provide a unified basis for both the propagation of learning signals and the allocation of exploration resources. AtomicRL couples Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO) with Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE), supported by a lightweight Progress–Completion Critic (PCC) that estimates atomic subtask progress and completion boundaries. PCC also provides progress estimates for constructing dense progress-based shaping rewards (PBSR). SAPO modulates TD-residual propagation in advantage estimation with a soft gate conditioned on semantic boundaries. Within each atomic subtask, it preserves standard GAE trace decay; across subtask boundaries, it maintains propagation between successful subtasks while attenuating residuals from failed subtasks. By leaving one-step TD residuals and value bootstrapping unchanged, SAPO reduces failure interference while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and successful subtask dependencies. BATE tracks the mastery of each subtask via a moving average of its completion rate, jointly adjusts the sampling weight of full tasks and the strength of subtask-level entropy regularization, directing interaction and exploration resources toward bottleneck subtasks. Finally, to support physical deployment, we develop an automated Real2Sim2Real pipeline. Given a single real-world multimodal demonstration and the required auxiliary information, the pipeline reconstructs an interactive simulation environment. It connects simulation-based RL with real-robot deployment, shifting costly physical trial-and-error to parallel simulation with reproducible resets. We conduct extensive experiments in both simulation and the real world. On LIBERO-LONG~ liu2023liberobenchmarkingknowledgetransfer AtomicRL achieves success rates of 99.0 with ~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld and 98.8 with OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing , improving over PPO by 3.6 and 4.0 . On CALVIN ABC-D~ mees2022calvinbenchmarklanguageconditionedpolicy , the average completed sequence length improves from 3.56 to 4.56, while the success rate of completing full five-subtask chain improves by 9.5 over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further yields an average improvement of 21.3 on real-robot long-horizon tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of AtomicRL for long-horizon VLA reinforcement learning. Overall, our contributions are as follows: We introduce AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure for long-horizon robotic manipulation. We propose SAPO to mitigate cross-subtask credit interference and BATE to adaptively direct task sampling and exploration toward bottleneck subtasks. We develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that streamlines simulation construction and RL training for efficient real-robot deployment. We validate the effectiveness of AtomicRL through extensive experiments conducted in both simulated environments and real-world robots. Related Work sec:related_work Reinforcement Learning for VLA Models Reinforcement learning (RL) optimizes policies through environment interaction and task-level feedback. Recent work has explored both offline and online RL paradigms for VLA policies. Offline RL approaches leverage task feedback to enable continued policy improvement~ huang2025corftefficientfinetuningvisionlanguageaction, zhang2025grapegeneralizingrobotpolicy, zhang2025reinbotamplifyingrobotvisuallanguage . ~ intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience integrates expert demonstrations, autonomous interaction data, and human corrections through advantage-conditioned learning. For scalable online training, VLA-RL~ lu2025vlarlmasterfulgeneralrobotic and SimpleVLA-RL~ li2026simplevla explore frameworks for continually improving VLA policies through environment interaction, while RL4VLA~ liu2026rlbringvlageneralization systematically investigates how different RL algorithms affect VLA generalization. Furthermore, Flow Q-Learning~ park2025flowqlearning , Flow-GRPO~ liu2025flowgrpotrainingflowmatching and ~ chen2026pitextttrlonlinerlfinetuning investigate online RL fine-tuning for flow-matching policies, addressing challenges in action likelihood computation and exploration. RL for long-horizon manipulation introduces additional challenges due to sparse and delayed task feedback~ chen2026sarmstageawarerewardmodeling, li2025grrlgoingdexterousprecise, dalal2024planseqlearnlanguagemodelguided . STARE-VLA~ xu2025starevlaprogressivestageawarereinforcement exploits the semantic stage structure of trajectories to perform stage-level preference optimization and reward shaping, while IG-RFT~ su2026igrftinteractionguidedrlframework combines trajectory-level and subtask-level rewards to provide intermediate guidance. However, dense reward shaping provides useful process guidance over long-horizon trajectories, but cannot eliminate the spurious interference caused by later-stage failures. In contrast, AtomicRL gates the propagation of advantage signals at the semantic boundaries of atomic tasks to prevent cross-task interference from unreliable signals, while allocating the exploration budget to bottleneck atomic tasks to improve the efficiency of long-horizon RL. Online Reinforcement Learning in Real World Online reinforcement learning for real-world manipulation is constrained by interaction costs and safety risks. To reduce reliance on real-robot trial and error, some research focuses on learning action-conditioned world models and optimizing policies through imagined interactions~ gigaworldteam2025gigaworld0worldmodelsdata, li2025roboticworldmodelneural, zhang2026practicalworldmodelbasedreinforcement, jiang2026world4rldiffusionworldmodels . WoVR~ jiang2026wovrworldmodelsreliable addresses prediction errors and their accumulation to improve the reliability of model-generated rollouts for VLA reinforcement fine-tuning , while PlayWorld~ yin2026playworldlearningrobotworld and RISE~ yang2026riseselfimprovingrobotpolicy learn world models from autonomous robot interactions and transfers policies trained through model-based reinforcement learning to real hardware. Although world models can effectively capture short-term dynamics, long-horizon predictions still exhibit visual distortions and action–state inconsistencies. Other studies adopt an explicit Real2Sim2Real method, combining real-scene reconstruction with physics simulation to provide interactive environments for policy optimization~ li2025pinwmlearningphysicsinformedworld, wang2026phys2realfusingvlmpriors . GSWorld~ jiang2025gsworldclosedloopphotorealisticsimulation integrates Gaussian-on-Mesh assets with physics engines to support visually faithful policy training, while RialTo~ torne2024reconcilingrealitysimulationrealtosimtoreal constructs digital twins of real-world environments and uses reinforcement learning in simulation to improve policy robustness. However, constructing environments requires coordinating scene reconstruction, physical asset preparation, and control alignment, making it complex and costly to reproduce. AtomicRL introduces an automated Real2Sim2Real pipeline that uses only a single demonstration to reconstruct a real-world manipulation scene as an interactive simulation environment for long-horizon online RL. The trained policies are then transferred to physical robots for evaluation. Method Overview As illustrated in Figure~ pipline , AtomicRL integrates semantic-aware credit assignment and bottleneck-adaptive exploration for long-horizon robotic manipulation. Specifically, SAPO modulates credit propagation across atomic subtasks (Section~ sec:sapo ), while bottleneck-adaptive targeted exploration adjusts full-task trajectory sampling and local exploration incentives (Section~ sec:exploration ).

title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration
summary: Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively. Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student--teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student's on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ~2x higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses ~100x fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by +40% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.

Practical Implementation Initialization. We initialize with privileged expert trajectories. The initial policy is therefore trained without contextual information and resembles naive student--teacher distillation; see Section~ sec:tsd . Deployment. At deployment, the policy starts from a null context, (see Algorithm~ alg:deploy ). For evaluations longer than the training context length, we use a sliding window. Context-length curriculum. At each iteration , the policy is rolled out for episodes, inducing a curriculum on rollout horizons. As the horizon expands, the student can eliminate task instances that are inconsistent with its history over a longer horizon, making exploration efficient. This also makes our method more sample-efficient, and we discuss this further in Appendix app:curriculum_ablation . How does work on arbitrary POMDPs? sec:pomdp We described in a BAMDP, where a latent variable remains fixed across multiple episodes. In a general POMDP, the hidden state evolves within a single episode. For example, in a locally observed maze, the agent does not observe its global position, and this hidden position changes after every move. At test time, the policy interacts with the environment for a single episode over a fixed horizon . As the underlying state changes at each step, the agent faces a branching inference problem: each action and observation changes which hidden states remain plausible. Thus, instead of coverage over repeated episodes for a fixed , we need coverage over on-policy histories across timesteps . In practice (see Algorithm~ alg:method2 ), samples a timestep , rolls out the student to produce an on-policy history , and queries the expert from the reached state, producing a partial trajectory that generates the queries and action labels (similar to takeovers in~ kelly2019hg ). The resulting tuples train the policy to map its history to actions that are optimal for the hidden state under that history. At the takeover step, it approximates , and over the future steps, the expert trajectory teaches it to follow one hypothesis rather than dithering. For example, in the maze, after each move, the local observations and rewards prune some possible positions while keeping others plausible. Further, we induce a curriculum in the context horizon by iteratively biasing the sampled timestep toward longer horizons. Thus, we adapt the method to a POMDP: collect on-policy histories, then use privileged labels to teach it how to guide future behavior.

title: CW-WAM: A Structured Contact-Wrench World Action Model for Force-Sensitive Manipulation
summary: Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by visual observations. We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion-force control, it contains a unified interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned motion-wrench chunks as control references. A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion-wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow-fast control system that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input. It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads. title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
summary: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.

Introduction World models predict how a scene evolves given its current state and the intended actions of the agents within it. Trained on internet-scale data, video-based world models bruce2024genie,yang2023learning,team2026advancing,agarwal2026cosmos are now able to generate photorealistic visual predictions of complex scene dynamics that are difficult to model with traditional physics engines. Modeling the world in image space is thus becoming a promising alternative to hand-built physics modeling in such areas as robotics hou2026world and autonomous driving feng2025survey . Existing world models usually generate predictions from the current frame or a short visual history. However, such observations may leave the underlying physical properties unconstrained, forcing the world models to guess a future state among multiple possible ones. For example, an opaque bottle appears identical whether or not it is filled with water, yet it will respond differently under identical actuation. A world model that relies only on empirical priors over object category or appearance will produce incorrect predictions in such scenarios, limiting its applicability in downstream applications that require accurate dynamics~ zhou2025dino,quevedo2026worldgym . This motivates calibrating the world model to the hidden physical properties of each scene. A natural way to resolve this physics ambiguity is to physically interact with the scene to infer its hidden properties, similar to how we humans would do for an object with unknown properties. Inspired by this, prior system identification methods~ wu2015galileo,yu2017preparing,kumar2021rma attempt to construct accurate physical models with closed-form equations and fit the predefined physics parameters to the in-situ interaction data. However, real-world systems exhibit complex, coupled physics factors, thus building a geometric model or formulating closed-form equations can be challenging. Hence, to adapt to each deployment setting, existing world models~ gao2026dreamdojo are typically finetuned on a small set of in-house data, which is computationally expensive. To this end, we propose , a method for in-context Physics Calibration for World models. Inspired by the in-context learning capabilities of large sequence models~ brown2020language,bar2022visual , we prompt world models with a sequence of observation-action pairs collected in the test environment (i.e., an environment whose physics configuration is unknown) for physics calibration. Our in-context prompting method sidesteps both the need for human effort to build analytical physics simulators for system identification and expensive model finetuning. Our method requires only an exploratory interaction clip without any gradient descent steps. compresses the interaction sequence into a compact physics descriptor token that conditions the world model. The entire system is trained end-to-end with only a video prediction objective, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator. At test time, first extracts the descriptor from a few exploratory interactions with the test scene (e.g., via random exploration or scripted policies). This descriptor then conditions all subsequent rollouts in that scene, enabling the world model to generate physically consistent predictions in novel configurations without any test-time weight updates. Physics Descriptors Learned from Video Alone: We introduce a physics descriptor token that grounds the world model in hidden physical properties. It is learned end-to-end from video prediction alone, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator. World models predict future states conditioned on current observations and agent actions, serving as an increasingly foundational framework for robotics~ li2025comprehensive,hou2026world . For example, they are scalable neural simulators, enabling low-cost policy evaluation without real-world execution~ guo2026ctrl,gao2026dreamdojo,wang2026interactive,team2025evaluating,tseng2025scalable . Through future imagination, world models can also substantially improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning~ hafner2019learning,hansen2022temporal,seo2023masked,wu2023daydreamer and facilitate policy learning~ saxena2026nostra,luo2025grounding . Moreover, optimizing action sequences with world models enables embodied agents to complete novel tasks via visual trajectory planning~ zhou2025dino,assran2025v,wang2024driving . However, existing methods typically condition only on the current frame or a narrow observation history, assuming that these observations suffice to identify the underlying transition dynamics of the test scene. As a result, predictions tend to suffer from severe drift if latent physical properties vary across test scenes. In this work, we ground model predictions in the actual test-scene dynamics by introducing an additional in-context interaction prompt collected within the test scene as input to the world model, substantially enhancing the prediction accuracy and visual planning performance. In-Context Learning in Physical AI. Context can serve embodied agents in various forms. For example, it can adapt a robot policy to test-scene dynamics by conditioning directly on execution history or by explicitly recovering physical parameters~ lee2020learning,kumar2021rma,liu2025locoformer,zhang2025dynamics . Another role is in-context policy learning, where task demonstrations steer actions either through structured representations such as keypoints and graphs~ di2024keypoint, vosylius2025instant, hwang2024promptable or raw video-action pairs~ fu2024context, shah2025mimicdroid, ding2026contextflow , and in-context reinforcement learning~ lee2023supervised, lu2023structured . Most recently, context has been applied to action-conditioned world models by prepending context prefixes to adapt to new camera viewpoints or embodiments~ yang2026syncworld . However, prior works focus on policy adaptation, require privileged physical priors, or prepend raw context frames at high computational cost. In contrast, we use context to enable physics-grounded future prediction in world models, introducing a compact physics descriptor token to minimize computational overhead while maintaining high prediction accuracy and rollout efficiency. Physics-Aware Video Generation. Video generative models have advanced rapidly~ yang2025cogvideox,zheng2025open,chen2026sana , with widespread commercial deployment~ seedance2026seedance,wan2025wan . However, their adherence to physical laws remains limited~ motamed2026generative,upadhyay2026worldbench,bansal2025videophy,meng2024towards . Recent efforts seek to improve physical awareness in video models by incorporating explicit physics equations or parameters in the generation process~ zhang2024physdreamer,wang2026physctrl,yuan2026newtongen,wang2026wisa , coupling with external physics simulators~ liu2024physgen,xie2025physanimator,foo2026physical , leveraging foundation models~ xue2025phyt2v,zhang2026videorepa , or optimizing handcrafted rewards~ zhang2026physrvg,li2025pisa . However, these approaches either rely on analytical formulations and are restricted to a pre-defined set of physics properties, or focus on learning general physics and tend to fail in scenarios that require fine-grained instance-level physics grounding. In comparison, our work focuses on calibrating action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics of a test scene from an exploratory interaction prompt, operating entirely end-to-end without prior assumptions or ground-truth supervision of the environment's underlying physics. At each step, the agent receives a high-dimensional visual observation (and an optional proprioceptive state ) and executes a control action . title: Agentic World Action Models
summary: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.

Predicting the world and/or actions in general can also be expensive, especially as it can be difficult to establish limits on how many degrees of freedom need to be “world modeled” (or teleoperated, in the supervised setting). Agentic robot systems provide complementary structure to WAMs: a programmatic harness that selects reusable skills and tools, binds them to the current scene, tracks progress, and replans as observations change~ liang2023code,fu2026capx,zhang2026playfulagenticrobotlearning, xiao2026enpireagenticrobotpolicy,lu2026aspire . title: AutoPhyX: Automatic Text-Condition Physics Property Generation
summary: High-fidelity 4D physical simulation requires accurate physical parameter assignments that align with diverse material properties. Previous methods struggle with critical bottlenecks: they either rely on computationally intensive per-scene optimization or predict parameters from purely visual inputs. The latter suffers from inherent ambiguity, e.g., the inability to distinguish the stiffness of rubber from its appearance alone. To bridge this gap, we propose AutoPhyX, a text-conditioned framework for predicting spatially-varying physical properties. Since training robust feed-forward models requires fine-grained supervision, we first introduce a novel part-controllable data generation pipeline that decomposes complex 3D assets into semantically distinct components and pairs them with physically plausible, diverse parameters and corresponding text descriptions. Leveraging this dataset, AutoPhyX employs a cross-modal modulation mechanism where text features dynamically modulate visual features for precise physical grounding. By formulating property prediction within a voxel field, AutoPhyX ensures compatibility with diverse 3D representations, including meshes, point clouds, Gaussian Splatting, and NeRF. Experiments demonstrate that our method enables physically plausible, text-driven parameter assignment in a single forward pass. It achieves high accuracy and robust generalization to in-the-wild objects, paving the way for future physics-intensive embodied and robotic applications.

title: Early versus Late RGB-Infrared Fusion for Counter-UAV Detection: A Comparative Study
comment: This version differs from the article published in IEEE Access. It includes revisions requested by the reviewers during the final review round that could not be incorporated into the published version
summary: This paper presents a novel strategy for UAV detection through visible (RGB) and infrared (IR) fusion, in order to improve accuracy and precision in harsh environments and weather conditions. In this research, two opposite approaches have been studied and implemented: the first concerns image-level (early) fusion, which merges two different spectra into a single image to which one detector is applied. On the other hand, the second approach, called decision-level (late) fusion, focuses on blending together the output bounding boxes of two different detection pipelines, aiming to create a common result that can be applied to both spectra simultaneously. Both strategies have been extensively tested in a dedicated environment, which included alternating low and high brightness scenes, different backgrounds (sky and ground), distances (5, 25 and 60 m), altitudes and zoom levels (1X, 2X and 4X). These tests allowed for the assessment of actual detection capabilities and system reliability in real-world applications. Furthermore, the two fusion strategies were evaluated and compared over a set of aligned images in order to highlight the better approach of the two. The results indicate that early fusion achieves better raw performance, since it incorporates the thermal information from the beginning of the training process. However, late fusion presents an innovative and useful detection workflow that can be applied in cases of sensor or frame misalignment. Both positive and negative aspects have also been pointed out and discussed, in order to give a more comprehensive overview. Finally, the paper outlines implementation considerations and practical recommendations based on operational priorities. Overall, the findings contribute to the research in RGB-IR fusion modalities, with the goal of enhancing UAV detection capabilities.

Introduction sec:introduction nmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are becoming increasingly common in military and civilian applications. They can be used in surveillance, mapping and transporting materials. However, there are safety and security concerns which have to be taken into consideration, since modern UAVs might be able to operate in varied environments and evade traditional surveillance methods. In order to reduce these weaknesses, many advanced sensors are used in current scenarios. For example, visible light (RGB) cameras are widely adopted, as they offer excellent spatial resolutions and reduced costs zhao2022vision . However, they have problems in low light, adverse weather conditions Samadzadegan2022DroneDetection and crowded backgrounds. Concerning this particular aspect, the terrain texture may be difficult to separate from the drone's surface, since UAVs are usually made from composite and camouflaged materials. On the other hand, infrared (IR) cameras work effectively in low light situations and night scenes. Nevertheless, they have reduced thermal and spatial resolution and are expensive. Therefore, this research focuses on fused solutions for UAV detection, aiming to combine the strengths of both sensors skorka2022tradeoffs .\\ There are some studies in Computer Vision which have explored the capabilities of sensor fusion strategies in object detection systems sun2024visible . However, the Counter-UAV setting still remains an underexplored research area for fusion. Most of the existing approaches require significant adjustments and fixes to the sensors before fusion can be applied. In this paper, the following innovative fusion pipelines for YOLO-based Counter-UAV detection have been adopted and evaluated: An image-level (early) fusion that composes synchronized and aligned RGB and IR inputs into a unified representation for a single detector. A decision-level (late) fusion that processes RGB and IR streams independently and merges their detections post-inference. This research presents two logical strategies and the framework designed and applied for each fusion type.\\ Finally, in order to present a complete evaluation, extensive performance analyses have been conducted, including quantitative metrics (such as average detection precision, recall and F1-score) and qualitative visualizations through image samples. Synopsis. This work presents two RGB–IR fusion architectures for drone-to-drone detection using YOLO: an image-level (early) fusion combining synchronized inputs into a single stream, and a decision-level (late) fusion merging outputs from separate detectors. Evaluated across varied conditions, the study compares accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, offering practical guidance for Counter-UAV deployment. Background subtraction, motion-based segmentation and orientation detection were commonly employed in static-camera surveillance scenarios, leveraging temporal consistency to isolate moving aerial targets 9743918 . title: GeoMem-VLA: Internalizing 3D Scene Understanding into Temporal Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Geometric structure is essential for robotic manipulation and understanding the 3D world. Most VLA models rely on 2D representations of current observations, while geometry-aware approaches often require additional 3D information. However, geometry inferred independently from individual observations is often discarded rather than accumulated into a persistent task representation. Our key insight is that action generation needs a compact, task-relevant geometric abstraction that can be continuously updated, rather than a complete, renderable 3D reconstruction at every step. We introduce GeoMem-VLA, a VLA framework that internalizes explicit 3D supervision into dedicated geometric tokens and maintains them as temporal memory for action generation, without directly aligning the VLM's native visual embeddings with the teacher feature space. During training, a frozen geometry foundation model supervises learnable GeoPlan tokens through a geometric flow-matching objective over the current scene point map and future end-effector tracks. These tokens are integrated with the memory of observation representations, where historical information is retrieved, adaptively fused with current observations, and consolidated to retain event frames as the task progresses. At inference, the policy retrieves historical representations and fuses them with the current working representation to predict actions, without invoking the 3D teacher or explicitly reconstructing the scene. After benchmark-specific downstream adaptation, GeoMem-VLA achieves 98.9% average success on LIBERO and 91.10% / 91.24% on RoboTwin's clean/randomized settings. Across five real-world tasks, GeoMem-VLA achieves 78.0% average success. These results suggest that internalizing and remembering 3D scene understanding is a promising approach to robot control.

Introduction sec:intro Robotic manipulation requires combining semantic understanding with precise 3D control. Building on advances in large language models, vision-language-action (VLA) models have attracted attention for language-conditioned manipulation rt2,openvla,pi0,VLA-Trace . Most use pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for visual and semantic understanding and generate actions through tokenized prediction or dedicated action experts. However, their reliance on current 2D observations offers limited support for precise 3D spatial reasoning and decision-making that depend on interaction history. Recent work on 3D-aware VLAs has explored how to leverage the rich geometric priors of the physical environment spatialforcing, geopredict . Such supervision allows explicit geometric targets to shape policy representations that require explicit reconstruction during action inference. Memory-augmented policies, meanwhile, retain perceptual and task context from earlier observations memoryvla . Connecting these directions raises a central question: How can geometric supervision shape spatial memory that guides action? This places the spatial content of memory at the center of policy representation learning. We propose , a VLA framework that couples geometry-supervised representations with causal episode-level memory. During training, learnable tokens summarize the multimodal context and condition an auxiliary flow-matching head that predicts current-scene point maps and future Cartesian end-effector tracks. A frozen VGGT teacher vggt provides scene-geometry targets, while demonstration trajectories provide future motion supervision. These complementary targets train the tokens to encode scene structure and task-related motion. At deployment, the teacher and reconstruction head are removed from the action-generation path; the learned tokens provide compact geometric context for the policy. To preserve this context, we maintain geometric memory alongside perceptual and task-related memory. We further use event-aware training that samples temporally separated observations from the same episode while preserving their chronological order and causal access. title: CausalAlign: Causal Alignment of Video Generation Models for Consistent Ego-Motion
summary: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. Camera ego-motion determines how the viewpoint changes between frames and is essential for maintaining consistent geometry and trajectories. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment framework with two components. First, we diagnose how precise ego motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions, revealing a rise-and-fall pattern during denoising. Second, we strengthen ego-motion state in VGM by aligning the representations at the identified layers to a 3D foundation model through delta-token space. This space encodes the changes between consecutive frames, allowing the alignment to focus on ego-motion dynamics rather than static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign can largely improve motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness, while preserving visual quality. For example, it improves geometric consistency by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, with the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves the success rate of world action models (WAMs) by 10 points on mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields noticeable gains in embodied models.
full_text: 0pt 0.35em Introduction Recent advances in diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) have led to remarkable models such as Wan2.2~ wan2025 and Cosmos3~ agarwal2026cosmos . Trained on Internet-scale collections of 2D videos, these models can synthesize visually compelling content~ huang2024vbench,huang2025vbenchpp . However, trained to model 2D appearance and local motion statistics, standard VGMs struggle to capture 3D camera trajectories and to control viewpoint changes consistently across frames~ wu2026geometry,kupyn2025epipolar . We refer to these cross-frame viewpoint changes as camera ego-motion. As shown in Figure ~ fig:comparison (left panel), prior work has attempted to address this challenge by introducing explicit 3D priors or preference alignment~ wang2024motionctrl,ren2025gen3c,zhang2025worldconsistent,bahmani2025ac3d , yet generating videos with geometrically consistent camera trajectories remains an open problem. At the same time, recent work shows that VGMs can implicitly estimate camera poses from their internal representations, even when their generated trajectories are imperfect~ bahmani2025ac3d . This raises a more fundamental question: how is precise ego-motion represented, used, and retained within VGMs? This question becomes increasingly important when VGMs are integrated into world action models (WAMs) for robotic mobile manipulation: visually plausible yet geometrically inconsistent predictions of the future can induce systematic errors in downstream action prediction. As the first step, we perform analysis for understanding the ego-motion information within VGMs. Inspired by prior works~ alain2016understanding,meng2022locating , we adopt linear probing to measure the internal representations of VGMs and causal intervention to reveal the mechanisms of VGMs. Specifically, for linear probing, we define ``decodability'' as the amount of ego-motion information. Meanwhile, for causal intervention, we define ``causal effect'' as the extent to which the interventions on VGM can change the generation. Our analysis results demonstrate that both measurements exhibit the same trend, that is, increasing first and then declining, across both denoising timesteps and denoising Transformer layers. These results suggest that ego-motion state emerges as the denoising progresses, however, fades away at the late timesteps and the last few Transformer layers at each step. Therefore, ego-motion is already learned and represented in VGMs, increasingly used at intermediate stages, yet not well retained at later stages. We refer to this progressive pattern as ``geometric state forgetting''. Motivated by this diagnosis, our goal is to preserve and strengthen the ego-motion state within VGMs without compromising the quality of visual generation. To this end, we propose CausalAlign, a framework with two components: causal diagnosis and delta-token alignment, as shown in Figure~ fig:comparison (middle panel). First, causal diagnosis leverages linear probing and causal intervention to identify where ego-motion is represented, used, and forgotten within a VGM. Second, delta-token alignment supervises the internal ego-motion state at the positions identified as forgetting. There are two key challenges in our alignment: how to represent ego-motion with the hidden states in VGMs, and how to provide meaningful geometry supervision for such representations. For the first challenge, we adopt the idea of delta tokens, which was initially designed for improving the efficiency of the world model~ kerssies2026frame . We adapt this idea to measure the ego-motion via the difference between two consecutive frames. Delta tokens serve as a natural carrier for motion information while reducing redundant static scene content. For the second challenge, we construct the delta-token space by leveraging the pretrained 3D foundation model. These 3D models are capable of estimating camera poses, depth, and 3D structure, and thus can provide high-quality geometric supervision. A learnable projector then maps consecutive hidden-state transitions into this teacher delta-token space, explicitly supervising ego-motion state of the VGM. By aligning these projected tokens with the corresponding teacher delta tokens at the identified layers, CausalAlign transfers geometric knowledge to the locations where ego-motion information starts to fade. With our CausalAlign method, we fine-tune the VGM on the widely-adopted datasets, DL3DV~ ling2024dl3dv and RealEstate10K~ zhou2018stereo . To evaluate the effects of CausalAlign on VGMs, we establish a comprehensive evaluation protocol with three aspects: visual quality, ego-motion consistency, and geometric state retention. Visual quality is measured with VBench-I2V~ huang2025vbenchpp and complementary metrics. Ego-motion consistency is evaluated through motion magnitude, geometric consistency, and temporal dynamics, while geometric-state retention is assessed through probe decodability and causal intervention effects. CausalAlign preserves visual quality while improving camera ego-motion consistency, as shown in Figure~ fig:comparison (right panel). For example, it reduces reprojection error by 22.6 and improves trajectory smoothness by 23.9 relative to the base model. It also alters the decodability and causal-effect patterns from rise-and-fall to rise-and-maintain, supporting the improved retention of ego-motion state. Moreover, we observe that the improved ego-motion state can facilitate downstream applications, such as WAMs for embodied tasks. Specifically, our fine-tuned VGM raises success rate on RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 from 43.5 to 54.2 . These results validate our method with causal diagnosis and delta-token alignment. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We identify a pattern called ``geometric state forgetting'' which reveals the ego-motion state in diffusion-based VGMs. Through linear probing and causal intervention, our analysis reveals that ego-motion information is progressively represented and used during the denoising process, yet not retained at the late stages of denoising. (2) We propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment method that aims to preserve ego-motion state at the VGM layers identified by our causal analysis. Our technical innovation lies in adapting the idea of delta tokens to strengthen ego-motion consistency via 3D foundation models. (3) Extensive experiments and comprehensive metrics validate the benefits of our method. It largely improves ego-motion consistency, better preserves ego-motion state during denoising, and offers remarkable gains for WAM in robotic tasks. Related Work sec:related_work diffusion and world action models. Video diffusion extends image denoising to joint spatiotemporal generation~ ho2022video , while open backbones such as Wan have broadened its use~ wan2025 . Unlike image generation, VGMs require preserving temporal correspondences and scene geometry across multiple frames~ huang2024vbench,huang2025vbenchpp,ren2025gen3c,zhang2025worldconsistent . These priors increasingly serve as action-conditioned simulators or policies: Genie and IRASim learn controllable future dynamics, while VideoVLA, DreamZero, and LingBot-VA couple observations with executable actions; Fast-WAM shows that video co-training can improve action representations without test-time video decoding~ bruce2024genie,zhu2025irasim,shen2026videovla,ye2026worldaction,li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam . Therefore, ego-motion consistency is internally related to WAM and erroneous camera motion can corrupt the predicted actions. Rather than proposing another WAM, CausalAlign restores and strengthens the ego-motion state of the VGM to facilitate WAM performance. Our method elicits the knowledge that has been learned during VGM pretraining, providing an alternative route for stronger WAMs. Feed-forward 3D foundation models. Feed-forward 3D reconstruction has progressed from point-map predictors such as DUSt3R and VGGT~ wang2024dust3r,wang2025vggt to streaming models with temporal state. CUT3R recurrently maintains a metric-scale scene representation~ wang2025cut3r , while LingBot-Map organizes streaming context into anchor, pose-reference, and trajectory memories and demonstrates improved trajectory and pose accuracy over VGGT~ chen2026lingbotmap . These models provide camera and scene representations that can serve as supervision for video generation. We thus adopt LingBot-Map as the teacher model and study how its ego-motion state can be transferred to a video generator. Geometry-aware alignment and post-training. As summarized in Figure~ fig:comparison , existing geometry-aware adaptation methods can be categorized into three types. External 3D cache methods such as GEN3C and Voyager use point cloud or world memories for controllable camera motion, yet require additional geometric memory and may propagate cache errors~ ren2025gen3c,huang2025voyager . Preference alignment methods such as VideoGPA and Epipolar-DPO supervise generated videos through preference or epipolar feedback, without directly improving the VGM's internal geometric state~ du2026videogpa,kupyn2025epipolar . Direct alignment methods, including JOG3R, Geometry Forcing, and FantasyWorld, transfer geometric features into the generator but do not explicitly target at effective timestep and layer locations~ huang2025jog3r,wu2026geometry,dai2026fantasyworld . Complementary WAM methods leverage 3D, 4D, or action-grounded supervision to improve action representations without requiring auxiliary teachers at deployment~ li2026wam4d,zhang2026mecowam,yang2026fourdwam,fu2026fourdwamdriving,qiu2026agra . CausalAlign instead improves the internal ego-motion state of VGMs through delta-token space from 3D foundation models, at the locations identified by causal diagnosis. Method Method Overview CausalAlign combines causal diagnosis and delta-token alignment to preserve ego-motion representations in diffusion-based VGMs. We first conduct causal diagnosis to identify the layers and the denoising timesteps where ego-motion information fades. Guided by the causal diagnosis, we align the VGM using delta tokens in three stages. First, we learn delta tokens from a frozen 3D foundation model. Second, we train projectors to map the temporal transitions of VGM features into this space. Finally, we use these tokens to supervise LoRA updates at the identified layers and denoising timesteps, while keeping the original VGM backbone, teacher, and projectors frozen. In this way, CausalAlign strengthens the geometric knowledge encoded in the VGM without introducing additional computation during video generation. title: ClunoGS: Compact Language 3D Gaussian Splatting via Unified Optimization
summary: Language 3D Gaussian Splatting enables open-vocabulary scene understanding by associating Gaussian primitives with language features. These semantic attributes increase model storage, while most existing 3DGS compression methods are designed mainly to preserve RGB rendering quality. One straightforward approach is to apply sparsification and quantization sequentially. However, pruning based only on rendering quality can remove Gaussians that have small RGB contributions but are important for semantic prediction. Once removed, their semantic information cannot be recovered by later quantization. We propose ClunoGS, a compact framework for Language 3DGS that combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in a unified constrained objective. Semantic supervision is used during sparsification, and the objective jointly considers rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness. We optimize the unified objective with alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates. We evaluate ClunoGS on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation using the LERF and ScanNet-10 benchmarks. Under aggressive compression, our unified, semantics-aware formulation substantially alleviates the degradation of semantic representations caused by sequential compression and semantics-agnostic Gaussian sparsification. Ablations further show that jointly coordinating sparsification and quantization better preserves semantic accuracy than applying them independently.

Introduction sec:intro Open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding enables objects in a 3D scene to be localized or segmented using arbitrary natural-language queries, without restricting predictions to a predefined class set~ peng2023openscene . This capability supports applications such as AR/VR~ koch2024lang3dsg , autonomous driving~ cheng2024open , and robotic manipulation~ qiu2024open,huang2022visual . Earlier neural-field methods encoded semantics in implicit representations, but repeated volumetric sampling and network evaluation made training and rendering costly~ wang2023semantic,kerr2023lerf . Language 3DGS instead attaches vision-language features to explicit Gaussian primitives and reuses the tile-based splatting pipeline of 3DGS to render semantic feature maps efficiently, avoiding repeated volumetric sampling and per-sample network evaluation~ kerbl20233d,zhou2024feature,qin2024langsplat . Directly attaching high-dimensional vision-language features to individual Gaussians incurs substantial storage and rendering overhead~ zhou2024feature,qin2024langsplat . LangSplat mitigates this problem using a scene-specific low-dimensional autoencoder, while LangSplatV2 further replaces the heavyweight decoder with sparse per-Gaussian coefficients over shared dictionaries, enabling efficient high-dimensional feature splatting~ qin2024langsplat,li2025langsplatv2 . These advances reduce the cost of semantic feature representation and inference, but do not target compression of the underlying RGB Gaussian scene. Consequently, a complete Language 3DGS model still contains the original 3DGS attributes together with additional semantic parameters. Its compression must therefore preserve both photometric fidelity and semantic responses. Standard 3DGS compression often combines sparsification or pruning~ yang2024spectrally,ali2024trimming,zhang2025gaussianspa, hanson2025pup,fan2024lightgaussian with quantization~ navaneet2023compact3d,lee2024compact,navaneet2024compgs . Applying them sequentially decouples semantic learning from Gaussian selection, so RGB-driven sparsification can discard semantically important Gaussians that subsequent stages cannot recover. Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates this failure using LangSplatV2~ li2025langsplatv2 , GaussianSpa, and CompGS: semantic representations degrade whether semantic learning occurs before or after RGB-driven Gaussian sparsification. Our unified formulation instead coordinates semantic learning, sparsification, and quantization throughout optimization. To address this gap, we propose (Compact Language via Unified Optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting). The framework combines RGB reconstruction and semantic supervision with a cardinality constraint on Gaussian opacities and vector quantization (VQ) of selected attributes. Updating the scene parameters, sparse support, and quantized representations within the same constrained problem allows them to adapt to one another instead of inheriting irreversible decisions from a preceding stage. We solve the resulting non-smooth problem with an alternating primal--dual procedure. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,itemsep=3pt,parsep=0pt] We introduce a unified constrained formulation that couples an RGB--semantic task objective with Gaussian sparsification and attribute vector quantization for compact Language 3DGS. We develop a compact Language 3DGS optimization framework and solve the unified problem using an alternating primal--dual procedure that coordinates differentiable scene optimization, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates. We evaluate on LERF and ScanNet-10 using recent language-field baselines, sequential compression and ordering controls, qualitative comparisons, and controlled ablations. Related Work sec:related Language 3DGS. Language-aware 3D representations lift 2D foundation-model features into queryable 3D fields, with LERF providing an early NeRF-based formulation~ kerr2023lerf . Language 3DGS methods mainly follow two paradigms. Render-supervised methods learn per-Gaussian features or codes by matching rendered feature maps to 2D supervision, as in LangSplat, Feature 3DGS, GAGS, and LangSplatV2~ qin2024langsplat,zhou2024feature, peng2026gags,li2025langsplatv2 . Direct-lifting methods instead register or aggregate multi-view features onto reconstructed Gaussians without iterative semantic fitting, as in Dr. Splat and Occam's LGS~ jun2025dr,cheng2025occam . LightSplat and ExtrinSplat further replace dense per-Gaussian embeddings with compact semantic indices or an external object-group index~ bang2026lightsplat, ding2026extrinsplat . We build on LangSplatV2 because its semantic coefficients and RGB attributes share the same Gaussian support, allowing sparsification and attribute quantization to account for both rendering and semantic quality. Compact Language 3DGS. Recent work has explored compact representations for the semantic features in Language 3DGS. DF-3DGS separates RGB and semantic Gaussians and sparsifies the semantic field, while CF3 compresses feature Gaussians through pruning, merging, and autoencoding~ dai2025df3dgs,lee2025cf3 . CSGaussian progressively entropy-codes both color and semantic attributes~ tseng2026csgaussian . SCOUP represents semantic features with sparse codes, whereas CoSAG predicts and entropy-codes compact semantic bindings for individual Gaussians~ budimir2026scoup,jia2026cosag . These methods reduce semantic storage through specialized feature representations and coding schemes. General 3DGS Compression. RGB-only 3DGS compression reduces active primitives, attribute storage, or bitstream size. GaussianSpa and PUP 3D-GS sparsify optimized scenes using constrained or uncertainty-based criteria~ zhang2025gaussianspa,hanson2025pup . Compact 3DGS, C3DGS, and CompGS use clustering or quantization to reduce attribute storage~ lee2024compact,niedermayr2024compressed,navaneet2024compgs . RDO-Gaussian jointly optimizes masks and entropy-constrained attributes, while HAC++ and LocoGS model context or local coherence for compact coding~ wang2024end,chen2025hacpp,shin2025locogs . FCGS applies a feed-forward codec to an optimized Gaussian scene~ chen2025fcgs . Joint sparsification and quantization are therefore established in RGB 3DGS. title: Rethinking Video Autoencoders for Interactive World Models
summary: Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-21-cadre

Given past frames and an agent's actions, a video world model generates the next frames, and can be used to train agents~ hafner2025dreamerv3,alonso2024diamond , evaluate robot policies~ yang2024unisim , plan the outcome of actions~ bar2025navigationworldmodels , or simply play a game~ bruce2024genie,valevski2024gamengen,hu2026multiplayerinteractiveworldmodels . To enable all these applications, two different aspects have to be optimized: the throughput that measures the number of frames generated per second, and the latency that measures the delay between the action and its effect on the output. Throughput limits how fast a simulation can happen, whereas latency limits how reactive and faithful a simulation can be. Most video world models operate in the latent space of a video autoencoder~ bruce2024genie,valevski2024gamengen . To avoid designing an ad hoc autoencoder, many methods~ he2025matrixgame2,li2025hunyuangamecraft,zhu2026sanawmefficientminutescaleworld reuse the autoencoder of a text-to-video generator such as LTX-2~ hacohen2026ltx2efficientjointaudiovisual , Wan~2.2~ wan2025openadvancedlargescalevideo or HunyuanVideo~ kong2024hunyuanvideo . They thus inherit the throughput and latency that come with it. Yet, such autoencoders were not designed with the throughput-latency trade-off of world models in mind, and often perform massive temporal compression since it has low impact on visual quality. A typical temporal compression delays every action by at least 400~ms at 20 frames per second. Humans notice when their own movement appears more than about 230~ms late~ shimada2009detectionvisualfeedbackdelay , and interaction feels immediate only below 100~ms~ miller1968responsetime,claypool2006latencyplayeractions . This raises the question of how other throughput-latency trade-offs affect rollout quality and action following. To address this question, we propose , an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders built for interactive world models. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features, which sets the compression, and share a causal diffusion decoder that needs one or a few steps. To study compression across settings, we train the same world model, a causal diffusion transformer following MIRA~ hu2026multiplayerinteractiveworldmodels , on each autoencoder, in two domains: manipulation (by a robot and by human hands) and navigation (driving and indoor). We compare with the autoencoders of Wan~2.2, Cosmos~ cosmos2025worldfoundationmodelplatform and LTX-2, the image autoencoder DC-AE~ chen2025deepcompressionautoencoderefficient and the MIRA autoencoder retrained on our data. forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Interestingly, our study points to four findings. (1)~At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression, and a few-step flow model trained by progressive self-distillation is a good fit. (2)~In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model: patching inside the world model loses detail, and at eight frames also action following. (3)~Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions. In manipulation the camera is still, so temporal compression costs little while spatial compression is costly. In navigation the camera moves and the balance reverses, so it pays to keep frames and compress spatially, the low-latency choice. title: DepState-JEPA: Learning Depth-Grounded State Representation for Visual Perception and Manipulation
summary: Predictive representations for robot manipulation should connect scene geometry with the state changes induced by actions. Our intuition is that understanding what an action will change starts with understanding where things are: complementary RGB and depth observations ground a common scene representation from which to infer those changes. Guided by this intuition, we introduce \textbf{DepState-JEPA}, a dual-stream RGB--Depth joint-embedding predictive architecture that connects spatial understanding with action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, \textbf{DepState}. Built on V-JEPA~2.1, the framework uses depth both as a complementary observation stream and to ground both modalities in metric 3D space, aggregating shared information into DepState while retaining modality-private features for decoding. Ray-conditioned readouts predict local features without target depth; after an action-conditioned transition, the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features using the predicted state and fixed initial private features. Robot-state readouts provide recursive proprioceptive inputs; object-trajectory supervision and calibrated forward kinematics shape state learning through motion targets and joint--TCP consistency. Comparisons show stronger RGB-encoder transfer after RGB-D adaptation, feature completion, conditioned visual forecasting, and manipulation success. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth content, metric coordinates, and future-state matching, with additional control gains from FK regularization.
